Islamabad United snap up Matt Henry, Karachi Kings secure Adil Rashid as direct signings for PSL 12
items.description: Islamabad United have signed New Zealand fast bowler Matt Henry, while Karachi Kings have secured the services of England leg-spinner Adil Rashid as their marquee direct signings for the 12th edition of the Pakistan Super League (PSL). Multan Sultans have also utilised the direct-signing facility, bringing Australian fast bowler Lance Morris on board ahead of the player auction scheduled for January 23, 2027. Lahore Qalandars announced Sri Lankan batter Kamindu Mendis as their direct signing, while Quetta Gladiators have signed Lockie Ferguson. Islamabad United unveiled Henry in an announcement on Tuesday, adding an experienced international campaigner to their bowling attack. The 34-year-old New Zealand seamer has taken 199 Twenty20 wickets and is set to make his first appearance in the PSL after having featured in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Karachi Kings, meanwhile, have opted for the experience of Rashid, a key member of England’s white-ball teams that won the 2019 ICC World Cup and the 2022 T20 World Cup. The 38-year-old leg-spinner is renowned for his variations and ability to take wickets in the middle overs. Although previously selected by Multan Sultans in a supplementary category, Rashid did not feature in the tournament after withdrawing due to international commitments. He will make his PSL debut with Karachi, with the deal reportedly valued at around Rs6.2 crore. Multan Sultans have strengthened their pace department with the signing of Morris, nicknamed ‘The Wild Thing’ for his express pace. The Australian right-arm fast bowler has limited international experience but has represented Melbourne Stars and Perth Scorchers in the Big Bash League. His ability to generate considerable pace is expected to bolster the Sultans’ bowling attack. The direct-signing window, which opened on October 23 and closed on November 23, allowed each of the eight franchises to recruit one overseas marquee player who did not feature in either PSL 10 or PSL 11. Under the regulations, a franchise making a direct signing will see its salary cap increase from Rs45 crore to Rs50.5 crore. Each team can retain a maximum of seven players, including its direct signing, with the retention deadline set for January 13, 2027. Franchises retaining the full quota will be required to release one player from the highest price category of the previous auction into the general pool. PSL 12 is scheduled to run from March 18 to May 2, 2027, with 44 matches planned across five to six venues.

items.title: Govt reduces diesel price by Rs4 per litre, petrol by Re1 per litre
items.description: The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Re1 per litre and that of diesel by Rs4 per litre, according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs318 per litre and diesel at Rs353 per litre on Nov 25 (Wednesday). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation. The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: 2027: INEC, police warn parties against electoral violence
items.description: … INEC raises concern over electoral law violations; Disu warns politicians against sponsoring thugs By Kingsley Omonobi ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has raised concerns over violations of electoral laws by political actors ahead of the 2027 general elections, warning political parties to comply strictly with regulations governing campaigns, rallies and other electoral activities. Similarly, the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Disu, has warned politicians and political party leaders against sponsoring violence, recruiting thugs and deploying dangerous weapons to intimidate political opponents, declaring that the Nigeria Police Force would not tolerate electoral violence. They spoke on Tuesday at a high-level security meeting at the Force Headquarters, Abuja, attended by national chairmen, secretaries and executives of registered political parties, security agencies, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. Expressing concern over growing incidents of political violence and attacks on citizens and members of political parties, INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, described the situation as worrisome. He warned that when political actors could not freely assemble, organise campaigns or express their views without intimidation, the democratic process was already being undermined before election day. Amupitan said the commission considered it necessary to temporarily suspend its activities to participate in the meeting because of the seriousness of the security challenges confronting the country’s electoral process. “Political competition should not be turned into a battlefield,” he said, urging political parties to focus on presenting their manifestos, policies and ideas to Nigerians rather than engaging in violence. He stressed that strict compliance with electoral laws and procedures was essential as political activities intensified ahead of the next general election. The INEC chairman recalled his earlier engagement with political party leaders and members of the National Peace Committee on August 18, 2026, where he emphasised the need for peaceful political competition. He said the credibility of elections depended not only on the integrity of the voting process but also on the political environment in which campaigns and other activities were conducted. Amupitan noted that attacks on political party members and other citizens could discourage voter participation and weaken public confidence in the electoral process. He urged political stakeholders to operate within the boundaries established by the Constitution and electoral laws, stressing that the security and welfare of Nigerians must remain a priority. According to him, political parties and their supporters must recognise that the people whose votes they seek are the ultimate holders of sovereign power under the Constitution. He added that all stakeholders had a responsibility to protect citizens and ensure that political activities did not threaten their rights and safety. In his remarks, Disu assured Nigerians that the police would remain neutral and professional in handling political activities, stressing that every political party and candidate would be treated equally under the law. He declared that no political ambition was worth the life of any Nigerian and no electoral victory justified the destruction of national peace. “Our neutrality in the political process is non-negotiable. We owe allegiance to the Constitution, the law and the Nigerian people, not any political party or individual,” he said. The IGP said the meeting was convened to strengthen collaboration among stakeholders and address emerging security concerns surrounding political activities. He expressed concern over violent clashes among political supporters, attacks on campaign venues, intimidation of political opponents, use of dangerous weapons and disruption of lawful political gatherings. According to him, such developments threatened public peace, endangered innocent lives and undermined confidence in democratic institutions. Disu assured political parties and their supporters of adequate protection to exercise their democratic rights, including organising rallies, holding meetings and expressing their political preferences without fear or intimidation. He said the police had zero tolerance for political violence, irrespective of the political party, candidate or individuals involved. “The Nigeria Police Force will not take sides in political contests, but we will take a firm stand against anyone who threatens the peace. We will not protect political interests; we will protect the Nigerian people,” he said. The IGP warned that the recruitment, financing and deployment of political thugs, threats of violence, attacks on electoral officials and destruction of electoral materials would attract appropriate law enforcement action. He stressed that political office, party affiliation and personal influence would not place anyone above the law, adding that offenders would be professionally investigated and prosecuted in accordance with due process. Beyond the responsibility of security agencies, Disu urged political party leaders to take ownership of the conduct of their candidates, youth wings and supporters. He specifically charged national chairmen to issue clear directives against violence and ensure compliance across their party structures. He also called on national secretaries to facilitate effective communication and compliance with applicable electoral notification requirements. The police chief urged youth leaders to mobilise young people for constructive democratic participation rather than expose them to manipulation and political violence. He called on all stakeholders to demonstrate responsibility and place the lives of Nigerians and the stability of the country above partisan interests. Speaking at the meeting, former National Secretary of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Senator Samuel Anyanwu, accused some local government chairmen of contributing to electoral violence in states, alleging that they intimidated political opponents to advance the interests of state governors. Anyanwu claimed that some local government chairmen, particularly those appointed by governors, operated under instructions to deliver electoral victories for their political sponsors or risk losing their positions. He argued that electoral violence should not be blamed solely on political parties, noting that inflammatory statements and actions by politicians holding elective and appointive positions also contributed to the problem. According to him, some local government chairmen resorted to violence to demonstrate their loyalty and political influence, particularly during elections and the collation of results. “Some of these local government chairmen are appointed by their governors. They are given instructions before they are appointed or elected. They are all appointed,” he said. He alleged that violence often escalated during the counting and collation of votes, when armed individuals arrived in vehicles, intimidated voters and electoral officials, and carted away election materials. “When they come with guns and all that, INEC staff, wanting to preserve their lives, run away and leave everything. They carry everything away and go somewhere to write results,” he alleged. Anyanwu urged the police to strengthen security around polling units, collation centres and other sensitive electoral locations, particularly in areas identified as flashpoints. He also called on INEC to engage state governors and local government chairmen ahead of the 2027 elections to address the alleged involvement of political office holders in electoral violence. The former PDP national secretary cited experiences involving his party in some states, alleging that its members had faced intimidation and attacks. He, however, commended the Commissioner of Police in Enugu State for providing political parties with what he described as a level playing field for campaigns. Anyanwu expressed concern over the security situation in other states, particularly Edo, where he alleged that members of his party had faced persistent harassment. Also speaking, former Minister of Interior, Rauf Aregbesola, criticised the police and INEC over their handling of electoral processes, warning that lapses in election management and failure to hold perpetrators accountable could undermine the credibility of the 2027 general elections. Aregbesola expressed concern over the inability of security operatives to prevent political violence, alleging that police officers had, on some occasions, watched helplessly as suspected political thugs attacked members of his campaign team. He recalled an incident during the 2023 electioneering campaign when his convoy was attacked in the presence of armed police officers who allegedly failed to intervene. He said he personally witnessed two separate incidents in which policemen, despite being stationed only a few metres away, did nothing to stop the attacks. According to him, some members of his team, including himself, were assaulted while the officers watched without taking action. Aregbesola said such incidents raised questions about the commitment and operational capacity of the police to protect citizens and enforce the law during elections. He, however, acknowledged the police and other security agencies for maintaining order during the Osun State governorship election, noting that no injuries were reported during the process. The former minister questioned why violence continued to characterise elections in parts of the country, insisting that democratic contests should not expose citizens to attacks because of their political affiliations. He also linked electoral credibility to the security situation, arguing that delayed results, poor election management and doubts about the integrity of the process could trigger violence. Aregbesola called for greater deployment of technology to ensure faster transmission and announcement of election results, warning that prolonged delays in collation could create tension and suspicion. He maintained that a transparent and seamless electoral process would help reduce the likelihood of post-election violence. The former minister urged the police leadership to demonstrate greater professionalism and ensure that officers deployed for election duties did not compromise their responsibilities or turn a blind eye to criminal activities. items.title: Education Ministry says early BECE directive will not disadvantage gifted learners
items.description: The Ministry of Education says its directive restricting Junior High School (JHS) 1 and 2 students from registering for the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) is not intended to discourage gifted learners or limit their academic potential. The Ministry says exceptional students must instead be supported through structured mechanisms that recognise their abilities while ensuring their emotional, social and educational development. In a statement issued on November 24, 2026, the Ministry acknowledged that some children demonstrate academic abilities and competencies beyond the expectations of their current educational levels. “Such learners are an important national asset, and their talents must be identified, encouraged, and appropriately nurtured. The directive should not be interpreted as an attempt to discourage giftedness, innovation or academic excellence. Rather, it underscores the need for structured mechanisms to identify and support exceptional learners.” The Ministry proposed differentiated instruction, curriculum enrichment and specialised mentorship as some of the interventions that could help nurture gifted students. It added that academic acceleration could also be considered where professionally justified and formally approved. However, it stressed that decisions on accelerated progression must go beyond academic performance. “Any decision concerning accelerated progression must consider not only academic performance but also the learner’s emotional readiness, social development and overall educational interests,” it stated. The Ministry said the objective was to ensure that gifted learners receive opportunities to develop their potential without compromising the integrity of the national examination system. The Education Ministry’s clarification comes amid concerns that the directive restricting JHS 1 and 2 students from registering for the BECE could disadvantage gifted learners who are academically advanced and ready to progress ahead of their peers.

items.title: Ethiopia offers to host and facilitate inclusive Sudanese dialogue
items.description: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has proposed an initiative to host and facilitate an inclusive Sudanese dialogue involving all military, political, and civilian parties, with the aim of ending the war and reaching a comprehensive national consensus. He says Ethiopia is prepared to use its diplomatic relations and regional influence to help create the conditions for negotiations and a lasting peace in Sudan. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (Photo: pmo.gov.et) The Sudanese government has accused Ethiopia of supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), particularly on the Blue Nile front, and of allowing drones to be launched from its territory . Ethiopia denies the allegations. Addis Ababa, in turn, accuses Sudan of supporting forces of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which opposes the Ethiopian government. In a statement seen by Radio Dabanga on Tuesday, Abiy Ahmed says the initiative is intended to create a conducive environment for serious dialogue, end the war and divisions, and reach a national consensus that would lay the foundations for comprehensive and lasting peace. He stressed that the initiative was not driven by any particular political agenda and was not intended to secure interests or gains at the expense of any Sudanese party. Instead, he says, it reflects a genuine concern for Sudan, its land, and its people, as well as a firm conviction that continuing the war serves no one’s interests. The real winner, he says, should be Sudan and its people. An impartial approach Ethiopia says it is prepared to maintain an equal distance from all parties and provide a forum for dialogue based on openness, seriousness, and mutual respect. This would allow Sudanese parties to discuss their differences and reach agreed solutions through their own independent national will. Abiy Ahmed says he hopes the dialogue will lead to broad political understandings covering an end to the war, the launch of an inclusive national process, and agreement on arrangements for the next phase. These would include forming a broadly accepted national unity government tasked with restoring state institutions, safeguarding the country’s unity and sovereignty, and rebuilding what had been destroyed by the war. The ultimate goal, he says, should be a just and lasting peace shaped by all Sudanese people. He stressed that Sudan’s future was a matter for Sudanese people alone to decide, and that dialogue among Sudanese parties was the most effective way to end the crisis and establish a new national social contract. This, he says, should preserve the dignity of Sudanese people, protect the country’s unity and diversity, and place national interests above all other considerations. The objective was not for one side to defeat another, but for Sudan to prevail, state institutions to be restored, bloodshed to end, and the way opened for a future embracing all its citizens. Appeal for international support Ethiopia called on the international community, neighbouring and friendly countries, and regional and international organisations to stand alongside the Sudanese people and support their legitimate aspirations for peace. It urged intensified humanitarian efforts to ease the suffering of those affected by the war, including displaced people and refugees, and called for support for all serious initiatives aimed at ending the conflict and resolving the crisis. It warned against narrow interests and polarisation that could prolong the war. Ethiopia also confirmed its readiness to use its regional and international relationships and diplomatic resources, working with relevant partners to create favourable conditions for the initiative to succeed. Abiy says Ethiopia regards peace in Sudan as an integral part of its own security and stability, as well as the future of the wider region. “Sudan’s peace is Ethiopia’s peace, its security is Ethiopia’s security, and its stability is a cornerstone of stability in the Horn of Africa and the surrounding region,” he says. He expressed hope that all Sudanese parties would respond to the initiative in a spirit of national responsibility and put Sudan’s higher interests first. Interconnected crises Abiy says the war, destruction, and humanitarian suffering in Sudan deeply affect the Ethiopian people. He says the situation requires Ethiopia to adopt a responsible position based on the values of brotherhood, solidarity, and a genuine commitment to Sudan’s peace, security, unity, and stability. In his statement, he says relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have been built on strong foundations of good neighbourliness, communication, solidarity, and a shared destiny. They have endured despite the various changes and challenges experienced by the region. He explained that crises and political developments in the two countries had affected one another because of their geographical proximity, intertwined interests, and human ties. The consequences of Sudan’s crisis, he says, are no longer confined within its borders but have spread to neighbouring countries and the wider region. Ethiopia’s role in Sudan Abiy says Ethiopia has followed developments in Sudan with deep concern since the outbreak of the war and has made sustained efforts to end the fighting and create conditions for a political solution. He says these efforts are based on Ethiopia’s historic position in support of Sudan’s unity, territorial integrity, and stability, reflecting its belief that Sudan’s stability is essential to that of the entire region. He also referred to Ethiopia’s role in bringing together Sudan’s civilian and military components in 2019, following the December Revolution. Those efforts led to an agreement between the Transitional Military Council and civilian forces, then represented by the Forces of Freedom and Change. Abiy says the war, now in its fourth year, has expanded in its devastating impact and produced an unprecedented humanitarian cost, making an active role by neighbouring countries and allies essential. He concluded that Ethiopia’s interest in Sudan was based not only on security considerations and shared interests, but primarily on historic bonds of brotherhood.
