items.title: What It Means to Secure Elections
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The relatively smooth functioning of the midterms did not end President Trump’s threat to American election integrity. After initially accepting the results, Trump has begun calling them into question, and House Republicans have named the outspoken 2020-election denier Jim Jordan as their next leader. Ensuring a free and fair 2028 presidential election and a peaceful transition of power remain pressing concerns for anyone who wants the country back on solidly democratic footing. In this episode of Autocracy in America , the Democratic election lawyer and founder of Democracy Docket Marc Elias speaks about his work safeguarding the midterms, the continued threats to our democratic system, and why restoring the Voting Rights Act won’t be enough to solve our problems. The following is a transcript of the episode: Anne Applebaum: I’m Anne Applebaum. We’ve just had the most consequential midterm elections in modern history. Americans clearly voted for a different kind of government. But major change will require more than one election. In this season, we will ask what steps need to be taken to undo the damage the Trump presidencies have done to our political system and reverse the slide to autocracy, even as Trump himself remains in office. At the center of any functioning democracy is the right to vote. A representative government is only truly representative if it somehow reflects the will of the people. The surest sign of a failing democracy, by contrast, is a flawed, manipulated voting process or one that always produces contested results. Americans have been trying to manipulate their voting system for decades. The word gerrymander was invented in 1812 when then–Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry drew a voting district that resembled a salamander. During the Jim Crow years, some American states wrote laws deliberately designed to prevent Black people from voting. Other states have tried to make it harder for students or poor people to vote by limiting polling stations or creating obstacles to voter registration. But since the beginning of the second Trump term, the federal government for the first time became the most important source of voter suppression, not the states. Having urged supporters to attack the Capitol in order to block Joe Biden from becoming president in 2021, Donald Trump did his best to shape the result of these elections in advance. He used government funds to make election advertisements. He sought to pass legislation that would make voting more difficult, and he tried to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail voting by obliging the service to determine who receives a mail ballot. His Justice Department sued multiple states in an attempt to gain control over lists of voters, and they lost all of those suits. To talk about the 2026 elections and to reflect on how we can build a stronger electoral system in the future, I have invited Marc Elias. He and his law firm have represented dozens of U.S. politicians as well as U.S. voters in cases involving campaign finance, voting rights, and redistricting. He’s also a strong advocate of voting rights and of high voter participation. [ Music ] Marc Elias, thanks for joining me. Marc Elias: Thanks for having me. Applebaum: Since the election, quite a few people have remarked on how smooth it seemed to be. There was no “Stop the Steal” movement. There were no overt attempts to prevent people from voting, as many had feared there would be. I’d like to start by asking you about the work that went into that smoothness and into that success: What were people doing to prepare for the midterm vote? Elias: So first of all, there’s no question we had a free and fair election. But I think it can be overstated that there were no obstacles for people to vote and that the government and other actors did not do things to try to make it harder to vote and easier to cheat. After all, we had an unprecedented effort by the Trump administration to actually prevent, among other things, mail-in voting, to try to prevent California from tabulating all of their ballots, to try to prevent Alaska from certifying the election results if a Democrat wins. So the fact that those things failed are good for democracy, but I think everyone needs to keep in mind that those things were tried and didn’t succeed. Now, in answer to your question, what we do, the way I think about preparing for Election Day is you try to solve the big systemic problems and then the small local problems. What made 2026 kind of a unique election in that it was actually the federal government rather than the states who were posing some of the greatest risks to elections. And then at a local level, we are involved in a lot of litigation and a lot of working with candidates and local election officials to try to remove the friction points. Those friction points can be long lines. Those friction points can be a surge in provisional ballots, in people having their polling places closed, and those things can make a real difference, not just to individual voters and obviously to communities, but also to the outcomes of elections. Applebaum: And tell me what you were doing in Mississippi, because I know you were there in the days after the voting, or your organization was there. When you say you’re going down there to protect the vote, what are you doing? What’s necessary to do after an election to make sure the votes are counted correctly, and how can grassroots organizations or legal groups help? Elias: Anne, I’ll be honest with you. In the 1990s, I picked up an odd specialty of close elections, which, at the time, did not seem like a growth industry. I was involved in Harry Reid’s recount in 1998. I was part of the legal team for Maria Cantwell in 2000, so I wasn’t in Florida. I did Al Franken’s recount in 2008. I’ve done many, many postelection challenges. In 2020, I represented President Biden and the Democrats in defeating Donald Trump. So what the Elias Law Group, my law firm, does is we, in the postelection period, represent candidates. In this case, we represented Scott Colom’s campaign, and him, in Mississippi to make sure that all of the remaining ballots to be counted after Election Day were in fact properly counted. So in Mississippi—and this is a good example of the kinds of things that we try to head off before Election Day—they have fairly antiquated voting laws. They had a very large number of people who showed up to vote in person who were given what in the rest of the country we would call provisional ballots—in Mississippi they call affidavit ballots because they were not on the rolls. Now, these are voters who had done everything right. They should’ve been on the rolls. It was not their fault. It was the fault of the state having removed them. So in the postelection period, there was a process, county by county, by which the counties went through those affidavit ballots and figured out which ones should be counted and which ones wouldn’t be counted, and we were there on behalf of the campaign. I did not personally go, by the way, just to be clear. There were a dozen people from my law firm who were there. We are in a number of different jurisdictions, Mississippi being one of them, and we’ve had them in various House districts. Applebaum: And when you’re checking the affidavit ballots, what does that mean? You’re talking to the people who voted, or you’re talking to the officials who are doing the counting? What are you doing? Elias: It depends on the state. So in Mississippi, the vast majority, the overwhelming majority—let’s say there were 20,000 of these ballots, okay? The overwhelming majority, like, 19,000 of them, were what we call “self-curing,” which means that it’s just a question of the election official finding the right information in the county rolls to count it. So we were there making sure that nothing was missed, and that if there were judgment calls to be made, that we understood what the judgments were and could argue our position; then the Republicans would argue their positions. In other states, though, these are mostly non-self-curing ballots. In other words, the voter actually has to do something. So in some places, the voter has to come in and certify their signature is correct. In some places, they have to come in and they have to show ID. And so in those instances, we are oftentimes reaching out to the voters and essentially helping them figure out: Why did they vote a provisional ballot? What was the thing that was missing that needed to be fixed? And then we help that, and that is sometimes referred to as ballot chasing and curing . So that is also done in places where that is the dominant set of issues after Election Night. Applebaum: I think it’s something pretty unique to American elections, actually. I don’t know that there’s a process like this that I hear of in Europe when there are European elections. I don’t know whether it’s especially difficult to register to vote here or people get kicked off the electoral rolls here for more different reasons. I’m not sure what the explanation is. Elias: The fact is, it is unusually difficult to vote in the United States, and there are a number of reasons why that is. Some of them are historic, having to do with the history of discrimination in voting that still permeates a lot of systems. But Anne, one of the reasons is—and this gets into the whole voter-ID debate—that we don’t have a national election system, and we don’t have a national voter ID card. We don’t have a national voter-registration system, right? In most places in the world, and in some states in the country, if you move into the jurisdiction, you automatically get registered to vote. And if you then move to another county, you get reregistered to vote, right? It’s called “portable registration”—“automatic portable registration.” And we don’t have that in this country in most states, and we really don’t have it between states. So a combination of that, plus the fact that states have ID laws but there’s no universal identification document, means that there are more ways for voters to trip up. In states in this country—like, for example, Minnesota, where they have same-day registration—you don’t have people having their ballots set aside because they’re not registered. Because if they’re not on the rolls, they just register right then and there. But we have a lot of states that have very antiquated laws, and Mississippi, unfortunately, is one of them. Applebaum: It seems to me one of the big conclusions to draw from this election is that people are very fed up with the way American democracy works. If you were to talk about how this process might go forward if there were a movement or an impulse to reform, what would that look like? Elias: Let me break that into two pieces. The first is that the Constitution gives states the power to set the time, place, and manner of elections. However, Congress can, through legislation, override most of those choices. So Congress could pass uniform legislation in this arena, and in fact, it has in some areas. The reason why we all vote on the Tuesday following the first Monday in November is because Congress stepped in and said, Hey, states, this is the day for electing members of Congress and the president . ( Laughs .) The reason why, for example, military and overseas voters are given certain rights to cast ballots in the way they do is because Congress stepped in and said, This is the way you have to do it . So Congress could pass laws to do this. It is a little oversimplistic, but not much, to say that we’re in a world, from about 1965 to about 2008, in which there was a bipartisan consensus to make voting more convenient and to modernize elections. I remember I worked on a committee to modernize elections, voter registration in particular, in the early 2000s, and it was bipartisan. There was no partisan valence to this. What’s happened is that since then, the Republican Party has largely come to believe that it is better off enacting laws that make it harder for certain modes of voting to take place, because of what populations use certain modes of voting. I sometimes say, “There is no such thing as a neutral voting law.” If you asked me to design a voting system that would make it more likely that Democrats would win, I could do that. If you wanted me to design a voting system, make it more likely that Republicans win, I could do that. If you wanted more people in cities to win, I could do that. If you wanted more people in rural areas to win, I could do that. People are familiar with this concept around the drawing of district lines around redistricting, but that’s just one type of voting law. And so unfortunately, we have been in this cycle in which there is not a bipartisan consensus to modernize our election systems on a nationwide basis. There are several proposals to do so. I think that there are more that frankly are going to be needed after this election that are unique to the situation that we now face. Applebaum: Do you expect the change in state governments to be part of voting reform? There’s quite a few states flipped, not just at the congressional level, but at the state-legislature level. Is that gonna lead to any kind of change? Elias: I hope so. I have been an outspoken critic of our nation’s voting laws. And I sometimes say that if there is any Democratic-controlled state that thinks they can’t improve their voting laws, they should call me—’cause there is no state that could not improve the experience that voters have. And unfortunately, there are too many states—because the people in power were elected under the laws as they are—that are just like, Well, what we’ve got is good enough . And so I would love to see a prioritization both at the state level, where Democrats control the process; at the federal level, I would love to see a prioritization of not just a reshuffling of some of the election rules and laws, but frankly a wholesale reevaluation of what the challenges are. One of the proposals you will oftentimes hear, and I’m not opposed to it by any stretch of the imagination, is people will say we need to reauthorize the Voting Rights Act as part of reform. And to be clear, the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act was atrocious and was a stain on the institution. That never should have happened. But I would challenge folks that if in 2026—with all of the experiences we have had, with all of the threats that have come from Donald Trump—surely we can do more and do additional work to simply restoring a law that was meeting the moment in 1965. I’m not saying that we shouldn’t restore the Voting Rights Act, but it’s not sufficient to the moment we’re in, in which you have Donald Trump at least musing that Republicans should take over the vote counting, and the Department of Justice filing lawsuit after lawsuit to try to undermine states’ abilities to run free and fair elections. I just think the medicine that we need at this moment has to be much stronger than what people have talked about in the past. Applebaum: Let me ask you about gerrymandering. We saw for the first time the federal government involving itself in gerrymandering out of cycle, right? It was something that used to happen after a census. Both sides did it, to be fair. Is there a world in which you could imagine either a national law or a norm that states began to follow where there were neutral forms of drawing state boundaries? I mean, other countries do it. Again, they do it in the U.K.; they do it other places, where they try to find, more or less, fair boundaries that represent real communities—towns or cities or villages. They don’t divide them in half or draw long, thin lines on the map. Is that a possibility that you could imagine? Elias: So first of all, constitutionally, it’s definitely possible. Congress clearly has the authority to pass a national law involving the criteria or the method or the timing. I think it is essential, and it’s essential for a reason that is not often talked about. You said something that is the common refrain that I hear, which is that both parties have always done it. When I got into law practice in the 1990s, what it meant to gerrymander was taking a physical map out of paper and laying it out on a big table, and then having a pencil and drawing lines. Today what it means is entering all kinds of data into a computer that can then draw a million maps, literally a million maps, in the span of a couple hours and give you every iterative version. If you want it that it will favor “this” kind of candidate, it can draw a million maps that do that—if you want it to keep these towns together or those towns together. So technology, frankly, Anne, requires us to tackle this problem. Because if we don’t tackle this problem, what the computing power is going to allow in the future is going to simply be impenetrable. I know that this cycle everyone says, Look, the gerrymanders are overcome by a wave . I’m not an AI expert, but I have seen the growth of the ability of gerrymandering at a technological level to be not the same thing as what you are referring to when you say Democrats and Republicans have always done it. Now, that said, Anne, the question of what reform looks like can be sometimes in the eye of the beholder. Sometimes people talk about reform as they want essentially fair partisan representation. If a state is 55–45, they want the districts 55–45. Other times they say, No, what we really want is competitive districts , so that whichever party wins, they capture a bigger slice of it. We don’t want 55 percent of safe Democratic districts and 45 percent of safe Republican districts. We want 100 percent of competitive districts that can swing from election to election. There are also obviously considerations of minority voting rights, and how do you factor in the need to protect minorities in that system? You may say, Look, we don’t want just partisan considerations to control here . We also want to make sure that within parties, within the overall electorate—that, for example, Black voters in the Deep South have the ability to elect their candidates of choice, and it’s not just a partisan fight . And that’s why these are not irreconcilable, but they do require having an honest discussion about what the trade-offs are between them. Applebaum: Yeah, gerrymandering bothers me a lot because it’s the one thing that seems to me really profoundly undemocratic. In other words, if someone’s running for election, and we know he’s gonna win because his party is designed so that his party will win, then you begin to have either members of Congress or members of state legislatures who don’t really have to care about what voters think. And this is how you get hyper-partisan politicians. This is how you get corrupt politicians, actually. Because if they’re not really worried about reelection because they’re gonna win automatically, then, it seems to me almost the most undemocratic thing about our political system. So anyway, I hope that— Elias: And then, and then by the way, Anne, we’re seeing some suggestions in some quarters that we move away from single-member districts. And we go to a proportional system. And we just say, Okay, you know what, Marc? We’re not gonna have districts in that state. Of the 10 congressional seats, candidates one through 10 who get the highest 10 votes will get the seats. Or they’ll run on party slates, and it will be based on the party share . Which is—you are more familiar with the European system than I am. But looks more like that. Congress has a lot of authority in this area to decide if they want a uniform standard. And in fact— Applebaum: So we could have some kind of proportional voting, at least within states? Elias: Absolutely. Applebaum: That’s interesting. I didn’t— Elias: If the state adopted it or if Congress adopted it. Applebaum: Let me ask you something else. Trump initially accepted the results of this election. I think on Election Night he said something about not challenging them, and then a few days later he started questioning the legitimacy of the outcome. You started to see poking up here and there people questioning various results. Does this look to you like something ominous, something that’s gonna build the way, after the 2020 election, we saw the “Stop the Steal” campaign building? Is this a threat to the certification of these elections and the acceptance of the new Congress? Elias: I don’t think it is a threat to the certifications. I don’t think it’s a threat to the new Congress. I do believe, and this is important, that we will see a growing election denial movement around the midterms in the way in which we saw it after 2020. We had an election. There were legal challenges to it that resolved themselves in favor of Joe Biden. There were certifications that followed that were settled with very few disputes at the state levels. I mean, a handful here and there, but by and large, the certifications then followed. And by the time you got to January 6, you had largely a discredited Donald Trump. What happened then was that frankly people like me, and I blame myself and others, we assumed, Well, the courts said these things and the states certified, and he was sworn in, and Donald Trump instigated a violent insurrection in the nation’s Capitol, and the national consensus will now be that there was a right side and a wrong side . And what we have seen since then, Anne—and this gets more into your area of expertise about sort of authoritarian movements—is the use of that as a way of building a core ideology. And I don’t believe that there is any reason to think that that won’t now follow suit as a result of the 2026 election. So people get sworn in, don’t get me wrong. But do I think that a year from now we will be talking about the “big lie” incorporating aspects of 2016, which it always did? Remember, Donald Trump set up a fraud commission after he won in 2016, and then obviously 2020. Do I think we will have elements of it that include 2026? Absolutely. [ Music ] [ Break ] Applebaum: Walk me through 2028. In 2028 there will be another presidential election, assuming nothing even worse happens. Then there will be another process of accepting it. How are you planning for that moment? One of the reasons I’m asking is ’cause I was very struck by the appointment of Jim Jordan, somebody who was a leader of the “Stop the Steal” movement, and Stephen Miller also, who’s now running the White House, also was an important part of the “Stop the Steal” movement. So there are significant figures from that movement who now are gonna have a lot of power inside the Republican Party and inside the White House. How do you see them playing a role in the next couple years? Elias: Jim Jordan is an election denier. Mike Johnson was an election denier. The judges who get put up, they’re not allowed to answer the question as to who won the 2020 election by saying Joe Biden, right? But, Anne, I’m gonna say something more provocative that I believe is true and important that people start to accept: We are in a constitutional crisis. There is a reluctance on a lot of people’s part to say we are in it. They want to say, We could be in it. We’re on the verge of it. We’re on the precipice of it . I just want to paint a picture for you, and you are an expert in foreign authoritarianism. You have a country right now in which we had elections because the president of the United States was defeated when he weaponized his Department of Justice to try to intimidate election officials with the threats of criminal enforcement about how they counted ballots. We had a free and fair election because the president of the United States tried to convert the U.S. Postal Service into a tool that would not deliver ballots. He is, as we speak, weaponizing the Department of Justice against his political opponents. And if there is ever any hallmark, I think, of an authoritarian regime, one of them is the use of the criminal prosecutorial state to try to discredit and jail or prosecute or harass political opposition movements. We have seen that not just in the run-up to this election, but we’ve seen it since the election. He continues to threaten Democratic senators. You have the Department of Justice and the White House and a U.S. attorney saying that if Congress does oversight investigations, they may be criminally prosecuted and investigated for that. And so when I look at this—and you asked me about the 2028 election. We are in a world in which the executive branch is operating outside of not the norms, not the usual, but outside of the Constitution—just is routinely operating outside of the Constitution without an obvious way for that to be checked—and that is the definition of a constitutional crisis and that is not showing any sign of abating between now and 2028. Applebaum: You represent Democrats, right? Your clients are Democratic campaigns or politicians or voting groups. How is it possible to make this argument that you’ve just made to me that we’re in a constitutional crisis? How do you make this argument in a way that doesn’t seem partisan? Is there a way to rise above this kind of conflict and find a way of talking about elections—maybe a technocratic way, I don’t know, maybe a neutral way—that gets us out of this kind of cycle? Elias: I turn the question back to you. When Péter Magyar was making these arguments, did you say he was a partisan? When Alex Navalny was making these arguments, did you say he was a partisan? I mean— Applebaum: No. So Péter Magyar was— Elias: Who do you expect to make these arguments if not the opposition movement to the authoritarian regime? And in this country, that happens to include candidates who are running as Democrats and people who self-identify as Democrats. It’s not only those. There are civil-society groups for sure, but it is a rather uniquely American phenomenon that we say, Well, we’re not going to accept that the opposition candidates and the opposition party has a voice in this because it makes it look partisan . Applebaum: Actually, people did accuse Péter Magyar—that was the leader of the Hungarian democratic opposition who’s just recently defeated Viktor Orbán, who was their authoritarian prime minister. They did accuse him of being partisan, but he managed to make an argument that was designed to appeal over the heads of partisanship to all Hungarians whether they were going to vote for him or not. And the question is how Americans do the same: How do we make an argument that appeals to Republicans, that appeals to independents, that makes the argument for electoral reform an American argument? Elias: Yeah. Fair question. The short answer is I don’t know. I know that there have been efforts to do that, and it is not the role I am going to play. I don’t think I am going to be the most persuasive voice to Republicans, given how much vilification of me there has been. I have been targeted. The president has called me names. He’s called for my jailing. In another country, if the lawyer for a political party was—if the president was calling for their jailing on the eve of an election, you might actually say that that would be a hallmark of an authoritarian regime and a constitutional crisis. So I’m not gonna be the most persuasive voice. What I know is that there are nonpartisan civil society groups that are trying to do just this. I know that there are former Republicans or even current Republicans who try to do this, and I cheer them on. I hope they are able to succeed. I view my role as slightly different. I am trying to buy time for them. I am trying to, one election at a time, prevent the collapse of free and fair elections. I’m trying to make sure we don’t have a failed election, because if we have a failed election, it’s very hard then to put it back together. So I feel like every two years I am trying to simply keep the trains on the tracks while others who have that space to do that work can do that work. ’Cause I agree, in the end, it’s not gonna be solved by brute-force politics. It’s gonna have to be a national consensus. To put it another way: The fever’s gonna have to break, and I’m not the doctor who’s gonna cause the fever to break. I may be the doctor who is keeping the patient alive while people figure out how to make the fever break. Applebaum: Actually, Alexei Navalny’s lawyers are in prison. Not that long ago, I met the lawyer—he had been the lawyer for Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya. She was the Belarusian presidential candidate whose election was stolen back in 2020, and he then spent several years in jail. So yeah, I think it is a pretty strong hallmark of authoritarian regimes to lock up the opposition lawyers. ( Laughs .) And actually, a third one: I was just in Venezuela, and I met Perkins Rocha, and he had been the lawyer for the opposition political movement in 2024 that was led by María Corina Machado, and he had just been released from jail. And actually, he was still in his apartment under house arrest, wearing an ankle bracelet even months after [Nicolás] Maduro had been kidnapped and theoretically they were under some kind of new regime, which isn’t all that new. So you’re right. The lawyers very often are the focal point of pressure precisely because they can use this legal language to convince people. So I take your point that you’re not a political figure and you’re not the one who’s gonna make the nonpartisan argument. But legal language, and even technocratic language, is often really important in these stories in convincing people, building support, creating the belief in the neutral institutions that make democracy work. So democracy needs neutral electoral institutions. It needs independent courts; it needs independent media. It needs these neutral things in order to function. And lawyers are inevitably part of that. Elias: I do try to explain in nonpartisan terms these are challenges that no one should face. And in fact, one of the criticisms that’s often made about me is—but from the right, which is not actually true—is they say, Well, you only sue Republicans . Ask the state of New York what it’s like to be sued by me. I sued them because they banned food and water in line, and I sued them and I won, and I made them pay our attorney’s fees. I’ve sued the state of California. I’ve sued any number of Democratic secretaries of state and Democratic states over their voting laws, because I do believe that there should not be anyone—whether Democrat or Republican, rural, urban, Black or white—no one should suffer the indignity of not having the ability to vote or have their vote counted. Applebaum: One of the other big issues in this election was campaign financing, the sense that billionaires and millionaires and people we don’t know are putting huge amount of money into campaigns and distorting the way they work. And I think we’re now finally at the phase where even ordinary people know. I mean, people felt bombarded in Texas by the number of advertisements they saw. They knew some of it was coming from Elon Musk or from other billionaires. This has been a subject that past Congresses have tried to deal with. They’ve been blocked by the Supreme Court. Is it hopeless? Is there a way forward legally or politically to solve this problem? Elias: The Supreme Court in the 1970s, in a case called Buckley v. Valeo , laid out a fundamental structure for viewing campaign spending, and it basically said that money facilitates and is a form of political speech, and therefore you cannot limit the amount of money someone spends independently of a candidate because it poses no risk of quid pro quo corruption with the candidate, and therefore it’s just free speech. And just like you can’t prevent someone from marching on the National Mall and yelling that Donald Trump is a crook, you can’t prevent Elon Musk from buying a billion dollars of television ads and saying that James Talarico should lose. That is the legal box we are in. I think we need to stop fighting the fight on the terms of Buckley. As long as those of us on the left are having this fight about whether money is corrupting or not corrupting, the Supreme Court is where it is. I think we just have to say, You know what? That is, in fact, the wrong framework . The entire structure is rigged in a way to allow unlimited money in politics. And what I would argue should go in its place is, rather than centering the speaker, we should be centering the voter. Because unlike other kinds of speech—unlike issue speech, where you’re trying to persuade elected officials—this speech is trying to persuade the voter. So what we should be asking ourselves is: What is useful? What is the thing that is going to make the voter in a better position to cast their ballot? And if people think this sounds wildly unconstitutional, I would point you to the fact that the Supreme Court has carved out allowing there not being electioneering close to polling locations. You’ve all seen that. You go to the polls and there’s a buffer around the polling location in which there can be no campaign speech, there can be no campaign signs. And that’s because the Supreme Court has recognized that there is this zone of sanctity around voting, that we need to allow voters to have a contemplative place that the courts have recognized. The Supreme Court has said that is an important aspect of democracy, that people, when they are casting their ballot, are able to reflect on the import of what they are doing as citizens—where they’re able to think about their choices and, in the voting booth, not be bombarded with messages. I think we should be extending that idea to this idea of unlimited spending in ads targeting voters or communications targeting voters, and it would allow for much greater regulation. It might not go as far as some of the European systems, where I think some countries actually literally have cutoff periods. It may not be that continuing to just try to rehabilitate the existing jurisprudence is not gonna do the trick. We need something different, and I am proposing this idea of a voter-centric approach built on this idea that there is something sacred about people considering their choice of ballots, and we need to give them the space from the cacophony of voices. Applebaum: And is that a task for Congress? Is it for advocates? Is it for lawyers? Who begins to push this idea? Elias: Yes, yes, and yes. The money in politics is not just bad because of the impact it has on Elon Musk and Donald Trump. I think people understand that. But it’s also bad because of the impact it has on people, on participating, on their willingness to vote, on their tuning out and cynicism—about politics, about them having accurate information rather than false information, about the issues and the candidates before them. In the United States, people say, You can’t have a democracy without the First Amendment being exactly as absolutist as it is around elections . That if you didn’t have Elon Musk able to do what he’s doing, you would not have free and fair elections. And I’m always thinking, Well, I think they have reasonably free and fair elections all over the world without this . Applebaum: I would go even further. I don’t think there’s any other democracy where money plays such a huge role in politics. And actually, yes, quite a number of European countries do have limits. You can spend X amount of money. I’ve cited this one before. My husband ran for the European Parliament, and his spending limit was 35,000 euros. Maybe it was 30,000. Anyway, it’s between 30,000 and 40,000. And when I say that in rooms in the United States, people laugh. You know, Oh, that’s ridiculous . But no, actually, that was the limit. ( Laughs ) And for that you can buy some posters. You can buy a little bit of stuff on Facebook, and that’s what everybody has. And so it’s a fair election because everybody’s spending the same amount of money, and nobody can outspend you. And somehow you manage to have a campaign and inform people and move on. You can still say whatever you want in your ads. You can still write whatever you want on your posters, but what you don’t have is a huge role for donors. And this is the thing that U.S. politics has that no other country has or few others. I don’t think any European countries have it. I can’t speak for every democracy on the planet, but the fact that every member of Congress has to have some relationship with donors or with people who give money, and some of them take PAC money, and some of them don’t. It doesn’t matter. Everybody has to have money for the next election campaign, unless they’re in one of these gerrymandered safe seats, I guess. And that means that you’re a member of Congress—you gotta have a million dollars every two years, and that means you have to spend a lot of time with people who give you money. If you’re a senator, you now need tens of millions of dollars, and that means you have to also spend even more time with people who will give you money. It’s not necessarily a corrupt relationship always. It’s not necessarily pay-for-play, exactly, but it’s a distortion of people’s time, and it’s a distortion of the way politicians have to think. They have to think like fundraisers rather than focusing their effort on: What do my voters want? How do I deliver it? What’s the best law? Do you feel the mood around this changing? Because I do. I just hear people saying it and talking about it, and there was something about the scale of the spending in these midterms, too, that seemed especially out of line for midterm elections, for Senate races, for primaries. Elias : I do. I think that for a lot of people, data centers is a democracy issue. People are really concerned about the data centers as part of a concern about their ability of them as members of community to have a say over the policies in their communities. Applebaum: We talked about what diminishes voter turnout, what represses the vote, but what would help promote voter turnout? What are the legal changes? If you were to make a list of things that would encourage people to vote more, what would be on the list? Elias: There are a few big things and a few small things. Number one, I think we need to allow people to vote the way they want to vote. There are people who want to vote by mail. We should let people vote by mail. We should make voting by mail really easy. We should have there be drop boxes. We should prepay postage for people who do it. We should make sure ballots postmarked by Election Day count if they come in a few days afterward. We should make it easy to them to get a mail-in ballot and to send it back. We should not require wet signatures, which means that young people who oftentimes don’t sign papers but digitally scan something in or go on the internet. There are a lot of things we could do to make access to voting easier. Some people want to vote in person. Let them vote in person, right? Let them vote early in person. I am kind of a “all of the above,” so that’s one thing. The second is our voter-registration system is literally of a different era. There is no reason why we have this complex voter-registration system. We have, with computers and e-poll books, the ability to know that if someone registers in one place and votes in one place instantaneously, that they can’t register and vote someplace else. So we ought to do away with preregistration requirements. People should be able to show up and register and vote in person. We should make a pledge and a guarantee and fund elections as needed to do away with long lines. One of the biggest reasons why people don’t vote is because of lines. And every time there is a long line—and I see the media celebrate it as a sign of democracy—I say, Well, how would you like to wait in line for an hour? It’s not a celebration of democracy; it’s a failure. I have promoted—and this has not been adopted anywhere, but I’m quite serious about it—we should pass a federal law that says that no voter waits in line for more than 30 minutes to vote, and if they do, the government pays the voter for their time. We have this with airlines, or at least we used to, I think, until it got gutted recently. But the fact is that if you wait in line for an hour, the county should have to pay you for the time that it took you to wait in line ’cause they failed you. They are in the business of making sure you can vote. And this brings me to the last thing. We need a voter-centric jurisprudence and a voter-centric understanding of voting. Voting laws don’t exist for the convenience of election officials. There are a lot of people, including my friends in the reform community and on the left and in the Democratic Party, who celebrate the election officials. I celebrate the voters. So the courts should be adopting a jurisprudence that treats voters and their inconvenience and their suppression as the most important thing in election cases, not the administrability, not the Is it too late in the election cycle? But it’s kind of what you were saying about redistricting—what’s kind of behind your sense that gerrymandering is wrong. It’s the idea that the voters are sort of afterthoughts in the process, and it should be the other way around. They should be centered. And I’d like to see the centering of voters in the way in which courts apply law. It would have a huge impact on gerrymandering, by the way, but it would also have an impact on voter-registration laws and these affidavit ballot laws and the college students who can’t have polling locations at their schools. All of those things would get thrown out because they’re anti-voter. And we would not be trying to balance, Well, yes, but it’s inconvenient for the state or, The state doesn’t like this or like that or, The election officials don’t have enough staff . And so I think that is where we need to go in any future reform legislation. It’s what I’d like to see the left adopt as a unifying theory of both voting rights, redistricting, and campaign finance, because I think it would actually center the debate about democracy where it should be, which is not on the candidates, not on the election officials, but on the people who we are actually trying to get participating. Applebaum: It would also solve another problem in the United States, which is that I feel that for different reasons, Americans right now feel this lack of agency. So their lives are organized by algorithms on the internet, which show them stuff whether they wanna see it or not. And data centers are built in their communities without their input. And so many things seem to happen very quickly without them being able to affect anything. And one of the—always the causes of decline in democracy is when people feel it’s pointless. You know, My vote is pointless, or my action is pointless, or I don’t have any power in the process. But you’re right that giving people the sense that, We want you to vote and your vote is important, and here, we’re gonna make it easier for you —it doesn’t solve all the problems, but it’s one way of making people feel that citizenship is important and it’s an important part of what you do and who you are. Elias: Absolutely. If you look at exit polls, the second-most motivating issue for voters in this election was the state of democracy. It followed the economy. It was above health care, immigration, and other things. And you cannot understand the public’s high prioritization of data centers or the Epstein files, which were two of the most salient issues in the election. Neither of those were economic. I mean, neither of them are primarily economic. Both of them are a sense that there are these group of people for whom the rules don’t apply, and they can just do whatever they want to your community. They can do whatever they want to young girls. They act with impunity, and that you as an individual are powerless. And in order for a democracy to work, there has to be a way that people can feel like by voting, it changes the material conditions of their lives. It changes the policy outcomes they experience. And I think that the data-center debate very much is about the disconnect of communities feeling like they have that power from elites who act like they don’t have that power. Applebaum: Marc Elias, thank you very much. Elias: Thank you. [ Music ]

items.title: La FRMF conteste la décision du TAS concernant la finale de la CAN 2025
items.description: La Fédération royale marocaine de football (FRMF) a annoncé son intention d’engager toutes les procédures juridiques disponibles pour contester la décision rendue ce mardi 24 novembre 2026 par le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS), à Lausanne, en Suisse, au sujet du litige relatif à la finale de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2025 entre les sélections marocaine et sénégalaise. Dans un communiqué reçu par Hespress, la Fédération a exprimé son étonnement et sa protestation face au fait que sa demande n’ait pas été prise en considération. Celle-ci portait sur les conséquences juridiques à tirer de pratiques qu’elle estime susceptibles de porter atteinte à l’intégrité et à la crédibilité de la procédure arbitrale. À cet égard, l’instance fédérale a évoqué ce qu’elle présente comme la confirmation d’un contact entre l’arbitre allemand Ulrich Haas et le président de la Fédération sénégalaise de football, 48 heures avant le prononcé de la décision. Selon la FRMF, cet élément aurait dû être pris en considération dans l’examen de l’affaire. La Fédération a également relevé que la décision du TAS n’avait pas tenu compte de l’orientation récemment consacrée par l’International Football Association Board (IFAB), l’instance internationale chargée des lois du jeu, et la Fédération internationale de football (FIFA), concernant le fait pour des joueurs de quitter le terrain sans l’autorisation de l’arbitre, ainsi que les responsabilités et sanctions disciplinaires qui en découlent. Cette réaction intervient à la suite de la décision du TAS concernant le recours introduit par la Fédération sénégalaise de football contre la décision de la commission d’appel de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF), relative à la finale de la CAN 2025. En conclusion de son communiqué, la Fédération royale marocaine de football a réaffirmé sa détermination à engager toutes les voies de recours juridiques disponibles pour contester cette décision. items.title: Jinapor faults Mahama government over GH¢34.6bn underspending
items.description: Damongo MP Samuel Abu Jinapor has criticised the Mahama administration over what he describes as a persistent failure to translate approved budget allocations into actual spending, warning that poor fund releases are undermining government programmes. He argues that the reported fiscal surplus of 1.4% of GDP was achieved largely through underspending rather than improved fiscal management, with several government interventions receiving less funding than Parliament had approved. According to him, the government had recorded an expenditure shortfall of approximately GH¢20 billion by October 2026. The gap rises to GH¢34.6 billion when arrears and debt repayments are taken into account. Mr Jinapor cited the School Feeding Programme, Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP) and Capitation Grant as examples of interventions affected by the funding gaps. He said the three programmes received GH¢1.8 billion out of the GH¢3.1 billion programmed for them by October. He also questioned why the GH¢50 million allocated annually to support lifeline electricity consumers in 2025 and 2026 had not been released, despite the same amount appearing again in the 2027 Budget. The MP said the figures raised questions about the government’s ability to execute its own budget, arguing that allocations on paper do not necessarily translate into resources reaching institutions and beneficiaries.

items.title: Orpaillage clandestin : de Siguiri à Kissidougou et Faranah, le grand retour des ressortissants
items.description: Depuis l’arrêt des activités d’orpaillage clandestin dans les zones aurifères de Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa, un vaste mouvement de retour s’observe en direction de Faranah et de Kissidougou. Hommes, femmes et enfants regagnent progressivement leurs localités d’origine, emportant avec eux leurs bagages et, pour certains, leurs dernières économies. Entre retrouvailles familiales, pertes financières, inquiétudes économiques et espoir d’un nouveau départ, cette vague de retours soulève d’importants enjeux sociaux et économiques. L’effervescence est particulièrement perceptible dès les premières heures de la journée dans les gares routières de Faranah et de Kissidougou. Les arrivées se succèdent à un rythme inhabituel. En provenance des zones aurifères de Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa, des dizaines de véhicules déversent quotidiennement leurs passagers. Camions-bennes, véhicules bâchés, voitures personnelles et minibus participent à ce mouvement qui prend de plus en plus d’ampleur. Selon les constats effectués sur place, plus d’une centaine de véhicules peuvent être enregistrés chaque jour. Le spectacle est saisissant. À bord de ces véhicules, hommes, femmes et enfants voyagent au milieu de matelas, de lits, de chaises, de sacs et d’autres effets personnels. Dans certains camions-bennes et véhicules bâchés, passagers et bagages s’entassent dans des conditions particulièrement difficiles, faute d’espace suffisant. Derrière ces scènes de débarquement se dessine une réalité humaine et sociale : celle de milliers de ressortissants contraints de quitter les zones minières à la suite de l’arrêt des activités d’exploitation aurifère clandestine. Pour beaucoup, Faranah et Kissidougou ne sont que des étapes sur un long parcours vers leurs localités d’origine. Les destinations sont multiples : Guéckédou, Macenta, N’Zérékoré, Banian, Tiro, Douako, Sandénia ou encore Kobikoro. Certains poursuivent même leur voyage jusqu’en Sierra Leone. Des familles entre soulagement et inquiétude Dans les concessions familiales, ces arrivées ne passent pas inaperçues. Pour certains parents, c’est l’occasion de retrouver des enfants qu’ils n’avaient pas revus depuis plusieurs mois, voire plusieurs années. Pour d’autres, ces retours nourrissent l’espoir de voir bientôt leurs propres enfants quitter les zones minières. Les téléphones sonnent davantage et les appels se multiplient entre parents et enfants encore présents à Siguiri. Certains encouragent leurs proches à rentrer avant qu’il ne soit trop tard. Au sein d’une partie de la population, ce mouvement est accueilli favorablement. Beaucoup estiment que le départ massif des jeunes vers les sites aurifères avait progressivement vidé les villages de leur main-d’œuvre agricole. Rencontré sur place, Fara Kamano considère l’arrêt de l’orpaillage clandestin comme une occasion de ramener la jeunesse vers les activités champêtres. « L’interdiction de l’exploitation clandestine de l’or, moi, je dirais que c’est bon. Nos villages d’ici, remarquez par vous-mêmes, il n’y avait presque plus de jeunes pour les travaux champêtres. Ils étaient tous à Siguiri dans les mines. C’est ce qui faisait qu’on achetait davantage de riz importé. Les gens disent que ça ne travaille plus au pays kissi, certains nous traitent même de maudits. Ils ne savent pas ce qui se passe réellement ici », témoigne-t-il. Avec amertume, il évoque les difficultés rencontrées dans certaines localités pour mobiliser des jeunes autour des travaux agricoles. « Dans certains villages de Kissidougou et même de Guéckédou, pour tuer un coq, on avait du mal à trouver un jeune garçon, à part les tout-petits. Ils n’ont qu’à revenir. Nous, c’est la daba que nous connaissons ici. C’est avec ça que nous avons vécu et soutenu nos familles jusqu’à présent », poursuit-il. Mais derrière cette satisfaction se cache également une réalité familiale douloureuse. Le même interlocuteur affirme que plusieurs de ses enfants étaient partis dans les zones minières. Selon les informations que lui ont rapportées ses autres enfants, l’un d’eux serait actuellement en détention. « Moi-même, j’avais mes enfants là-bas. L’un est même en prison, selon ses frères. Vous pensez que c’est avec mon accord qu’ils sont partis ? Mais quand un enfant se sent grand, il fuit. Tu ne peux pas aller le chercher. Ce que je demande aux autorités, c’est de libérer ceux qui sont en prison et de faire en sorte qu’ils puissent tous rentrer chez eux », plaide-t-il. Le retour des jeunes, un nouveau défi pour les communautés Si les retrouvailles suscitent de la joie, l’arrivée massive de ces ressortissants soulève une autre préoccupation : comment assurer leur réinsertion une fois de retour dans leurs localités d’origine ? À Faranah, certains habitants redoutent les difficultés d’adaptation de ces anciens travailleurs, habitués aux revenus générés par les activités minières. En l’absence de perspectives économiques immédiates, leur retour pourrait accentuer la précarité au sein de nombreuses familles. Ibrahima Keita, un habitant rencontré dans la ville, exprime ouvertement ses inquiétudes. « Les voitures ne font que rentrer et elles sont bien chargées. Des hommes, des femmes, des enfants et leurs bagages : matelas, lits, chaises et autres effets. Aujourd’hui, notre peur à Faranah, c’est de savoir comment faire la réinsertion de ceux qui sont en train de revenir. Ils sont habitués à l’argent des mines. S’ils ne trouvent pas de travail, beaucoup risquent de se retrouver dans des difficultés. Nous demandons à tout le monde de veiller sur ses enfants et de bien garder ses effets », explique-t-il. À ces préoccupations s’ajoutent les pertes financières enregistrées par certains travailleurs. Plusieurs d'entre eux affirment avoir abandonné une partie de leurs économies dans les zones minières, notamment des cotisations versées dans des systèmes de tontines. « Certains disent qu’ils ont tout perdu. Ils expliquent qu’ils étaient dans des tontines et qu’avec cette situation, tout le monde est parti. D’autres n’ont même pas pu récupérer leur argent. Ce que je déplore, c’est que si les gens n’ont pas été avertis, ce n’est pas normal. Mais s’ils avaient été avertis, ils n’ont qu’à assumer », déplore-t-il. L’arrêt des activités aurifères ne touche pas uniquement les personnes directement impliquées dans l’exploitation de l’or. Ses répercussions se font également sentir dans les circuits commerciaux et au sein des familles qui dépendaient, de près ou de loin, de l’économie minière. À Kissidougou, Fatoumata Diallo, commerçante spécialisée dans la vente de riz, témoigne de la baisse brutale de ses activités. Les ouvriers des mines constituaient une part importante de sa clientèle et lui permettaient d’écouler quotidiennement d’importantes quantités de marchandises. « Je plains les autorités parce que nos business ont été arrêtés brusquement. Moi, je faisais le commerce du riz et ce sont les ouvriers qui étaient nos clients. Je vendais beaucoup, presque un sac chaque jour. Aujourd’hui, on se demande ce que nous allons devenir et si un jour les activités vont reprendre », raconte-t-elle. Dans son propre foyer, les conséquences de cette situation sont également perceptibles. Sa jeune sœur, enceinte, vivait avec un ressortissant burkinabè qui a finalement regagné son pays à la suite de ces événements. « J’ai une jeune sœur qui est même enceinte. Le Burkinabè est rentré. Qu’est-ce que nous allons faire maintenant ? Ce n’est pas de sa faute non plus. Le jour où il partait, il a beaucoup pleuré. Heureusement, il a laissé de l’argent et quelques objets à ma sœur. Nous sommes tous revenus ici. Mais on se demande si un jour les activités vont reprendre », confie-t-elle. Ce témoignage met en lumière une autre dimension du phénomène : des couples séparés, des familles fragilisées et des projets de vie brutalement interrompus par l’arrêt des activités minières. Entre agriculture et tensions familiales, des avis partagés Dans les rues et les concessions de Kissidougou, les réactions face à cette vague de retours sont loin d’être unanimes. Si certains y voient une occasion de relancer l’agriculture et de réunir les familles, d’autres portent un regard plus critique sur les départs massifs vers les zones aurifères. Pour un autre habitant de la ville, cette situation devrait servir de leçon à ceux qui avaient abandonné les activités agricoles et leurs responsabilités familiales pour rejoindre les sites miniers. « C’est bien fait pour nos parents. Ils ont laissé les terres à cultiver ici pour aller se promener dans les mines. Certains hommes et certaines femmes ont abandonné leurs familles et leurs enfants pour aller à Siguiri. Ici, beaucoup de femmes ne respectaient plus leurs maris parce que, dès qu’il y avait un problème, elles pliaient bagage pour aller à Siguiri », affirme-t-il. Il attire également l’attention sur la forte présence des enfants parmi les personnes qui regagnent actuellement la Guinée forestière. « Toutes les femmes qui reviennent, certaines sont venues avec trois ou quatre enfants. Les papas, eux, sont presque tous partis. Madame, regardez vous-mêmes à la gare le nombre d’enfants qui sont revenus », ajoute-t-il. Pour cet interlocuteur, le retour des ressortissants doit être l’occasion de renouer avec les activités agricoles, de valoriser les terres cultivables et de restaurer les équilibres familiaux fragilisés par l’exode vers les zones minières. Après les mines, l’épreuve de la reconstruction À Faranah comme à Kissidougou, les véhicules continuent d’arriver. Chaque débarquement raconte une histoire particulière : des familles qui se retrouvent, des biens transportés dans des conditions difficiles, des économies parfois abandonnées et des lendemains incertains. Dans les concessions, l’attente se poursuit pour les parents dont les enfants sont encore dans les zones aurifères. Les appels téléphoniques se multiplient et les espoirs de retrouvailles grandissent au rythme des arrivées. Mais au-delà de l’émotion et de la satisfaction de retrouver les siens, une question essentielle demeure : quelles perspectives économiques pour ces nombreux ressortissants qui regagnent leurs localités sans aucune garantie d’emploi ? La réinsertion professionnelle, la relance des activités agricoles, l'accompagnement des familles et la protection des personnes les plus vulnérables constituent désormais des enjeux majeurs pour les communautés d'accueil et les autorités concernées. Car l'arrêt de l'orpaillage clandestin ne signifie pas seulement la fin d'une activité pour des milliers de travailleurs. Il marque aussi le début d'une nouvelle épreuve : celle de reconstruire une vie loin des sites miniers. De Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa vers Faranah et Kissidougou, le grand retour est bel et bien engagé. Reste désormais à transformer cette vague de retours en une véritable opportunité de reconstruction économique, sociale et familiale.

items.title: Le fait que l’arbitre n’ait pas mis fin au match Maroc-Sénégal invalide la décision de forfait », estime le TAS
items.description: Le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) a justifié l’annulation de la décision de la commission d’appel de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) concernant la finale de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2025 par le fait que l’arbitre n’avait pas prononcé l’arrêt définitif de la rencontre. Il avait au contraire ordonné la reprise du jeu après que des joueurs sénégalais eurent quitté le terrain pour protester contre le penalty accordé à la sélection marocaine. Dans sa décision rendue ce mardi à l’unanimité, le tribunal a expliqué que l’arbitre n’avait commis aucune erreur juridique en décidant de reprendre la rencontre après les incidents survenus dans ses dernières minutes. Il a estimé que les dispositions du règlement de la CAF relatives à la défaite par forfait auraient pu s’appliquer si l’arbitre avait prononcé l’arrêt définitif du match, ce qui n’a pas été le cas. Le TAS s’est appuyé sur le déroulement de la finale, disputée à Rabat le 18 janvier dernier et remportée par le Sénégal sur le score d’un but à zéro après prolongation. Plusieurs joueurs sénégalais avaient pourtant quitté la pelouse pendant près de 15 minutes pour protester contre un penalty accordé par l’arbitre au Maroc, avant de revenir pour reprendre la rencontre. Le 17 mars dernier, la commission d’appel de la CAF avait décidé de déclarer le Sénégal forfait, avec une défaite sur le score de trois buts à zéro, en se fondant sur les articles 82 et 84 du règlement de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations. Ces dispositions interdisent aux joueurs de quitter le terrain avant la fin du match sans l’autorisation de l’arbitre. Toutefois, le TAS a considéré que l’application de ces dispositions était conditionnée à la décision de l’arbitre de mettre définitivement fin à la rencontre. Or, celui-ci avait choisi de faire reprendre le jeu lors de la finale en question. Cette circonstance a conduit le tribunal à annuler la décision de la commission d’appel et à rétablir le résultat de la rencontre. Dans son raisonnement, le TAS a ainsi mis l’accent sur le statut juridique du match et sur la décision de l’arbitre d’en ordonner la reprise, considérant cet élément comme déterminant pour établir si les dispositions relatives au forfait prévues par le règlement de la compétition pouvaient être appliquées. La Fédération royale marocaine de football (FRMF) conserve la possibilité de contester cette décision devant le Tribunal fédéral suisse. Celui-ci ne réexamine toutefois pas le fond du litige sportif, ses compétences étant limitées aux aspects procéduraux. items.title: GNFS welcomes firefighter assault conviction but wants tougher sentences
items.description: The Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) has called for stiffer punishment for people who assault its personnel while responding to emergencies. The Public Relations Officer of the GNFS, DO1 Emmanuel Bonney, says attacks on firefighters, whether verbal or physical, must attract serious consequences to protect officers and deter others from obstructing their work. The call follows the sentencing of Sampson Azumah to four years’ imprisonment with hard labour by the Achimota Circuit Court for unlawfully causing harm to a firefighter. Azumah was convicted over an incident in which GNFS personnel were reportedly attacked while responding to an emergency at the residence of actress Yvonne Okoro at Adjiringanor in November 2025. Reacting to the ruling in an interview on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Tuesday, the Public Relations Officer of the GNFS, DO1 Emmanuel Bonney, said the Service would have preferred a longer prison term but would respect the court’s decision. “The Ghana National Fire Service stands by the comments that he made. We would have preferred a higher number of years to be handed over to the guy. However, sometimes we start from the bottom and go up. So we go by what the judge has given,” he said. He, however, said the four-year prison sentence should serve as a deterrent to others who may assault firefighters in the line of duty. Mr Bonney stressed that firefighters must be allowed to carry out their duties without interference, particularly when responding to potentially dangerous situations. He also outlined the procedures expected of members of the public when GNFS personnel arrive at a fire scene. According to him, anyone who begins efforts to extinguish a fire must hand over to the Service once its officers arrive, regardless of whether the fire has been brought under control. He explained that members of the public could be called upon to assist with specific tasks, such as pulling hoses over long distances, but must not independently approach burning buildings. Mr Bonney warned that fire scenes could contain explosives, including gas cylinders, which could endanger people who lack the protective equipment used by firefighters. He said GNFS personnel wear specialised protective clothing, including proximity suits, to shield them from hazardous conditions, while members of the public may not have similar protection or insurance coverage. “When we get to incidents, we ask them to go back, we give them a place. Probably when we tell the media, the media will adhere to whatever instructions we give them, but the public will not do so,” he said. He urged the public to comply with instructions from firefighters at emergency scenes, adding that officers would request assistance whenever necessary.

items.title: Face aux pressions de Trump pour un accord rapide, Zelensky mise sur le Congrès américain
items.description: Volodymyr Zelensky s'est adresse au Congres americain pour lui demander d'intensifier la pression sur la Russie si le president americain Donald Trump ne parvenait pas a mettre fin au conflit en Ukraine d'ici la fin de l'annee. Dans une interview accordee a Bloomberg, le chef du regime de Kiev a fait part de son intention de reclamer un important programme d'aide militaire ainsi qu'un durcissement des sanctions a l'encontre de Moscou. Selon l'agence de presse, cette declaration traduit la volonte de Zelensky de tirer parti des recents revers electoraux du president americain. Les defaites essuyees par le Parti republicain lors des elections de mi-mandat de novembre ont permis aux democrates de remporter la majorite au Senat comme a la Chambre des representants. Le nouveau Congres entrera en fonction en janvier 2027. Les intentions de Zelensky ont ete revelees alors que l'administration Trump a fait part aux responsables europeens et ukrainiens de son souhait de parvenir a un accord de paix entre Moscou et Kiev d'ici debut janvier , c'est-a-dire avant que les democrates ne prennent le controle du Congres. Selon le Financial Times , « les Americains exercent une forte pression » et « l'on craint » que la conclusion d'un accord n'exige de « tres nombreuses concessions » de la part de l'Ukraine. Moscou est determinee a trouver un reglement, la balle est dans le camp de Kiev Les declarations du chef du regime de Kiev temoignent de l'intention de Kiev de faire traîner en longueur les negociations de paix, en sabotant les efforts des mediateurs americains, afin d'attendre le moment opportun pour tenter d'obtenir soit des conditions plus avantageuses, soit un soutien militaire accru. La position de Moscou reste toutefois inebranlable. Lors du sommet de la Cooperation economique Asie-Pacifique (APEC), qui s'est tenu a Shenzhen, en Chine, les 18 et 19 novembre, Vladimir Poutine a souligne que l'Ukraine devait accepter les compromis proposes par les etats-Unis avant le sommet americano-russe d'Anchorage , en Alaska, en août 2025, si elle souhaite mettre fin au conflit. Selon lui, Moscou a deja accepte ces propositions et il appartient desormais a Kiev d'en faire autant. Le president russe a egalement souligne que Donald Trump et Xi Jinping avaient mis en avant les interets des etats-Unis, de la Chine et, plus largement, de la communaute internationale dans le reglement du conflit ukrainien. Il a reaffirme que la Russie ne souhaitait pas poursuivre les hostilites, tout en precisant que leur cessation dependait desormais de Kiev.

items.title: Reacting to Bilawal's remarks on 'brute majority', a section of legal community wants 26th, 27th Amendments repealed
items.description: A hundred members of the legal fraternity and civil society have called for the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments to be repealed, reacting to remarks by PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, whose party had made their enactment possible. The 26th and 27th Amendments, enacted in October 2024 and November 2025 respectively, were passed by both houses of the Parliament amid outcry from the PTI-led opposition. Last week, Bilawal — a strong advocate for both Amendments when they were passed — said the 27th Amendment was “passed neither through political consensus nor mutual agreement; it was passed with brute majority”, and that the previous one did have mutual agreement. He also questioned the current status of the judiciary, particularly in the wake of the 27th Amendment, noting that resignations of senior judges followed the legislation. Later, the PPP chairman clarified that he was “not disowning” the 27th Amendment, but rather noting that it did not enjoy the same “unanimous consensus” as the 18th Amendment and the 1973 Constitution. In an open letter on Tuesday, 100 individuals — mostly lawyers and also including activists and academics — called for both the 26th and 27th Amendments to be repealed. “Pakistan’s constitutional order belongs to its people. It cannot be seized by a majority that its own members admit was never theirs to wield,” read the letter, also signed by retired Supreme Court Justice Mansoor Ali Shah. The letter recalled that Bilawal “admitted that the 27th Amendment was passed neither through political consensus nor through agreement, but a ‘brute majority’”. It demanded that the “constitutional order that existed prior to the 26th Amendment must be restored”, adding that any future reform of the judiciary must come through an “open and consultative process”. The 26th Amendment carved a constitutional bench out of the SC, with its members chosen by a reconstituted Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP) in which judges no longer held a majority. A year later, the 27th Amendment turned those benches into an entirely separate court, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), which is said to have effectively dethroned the SC as the country’s highest judicial forum. It also made significant changes to the judicial system and the military’s chain of command , and granted immunities to government officials. Two of the SC’s senior-most judges, including Shah, resigned in protest the day it became law. Tuesday’s letter also called for reserved seats in the legislative houses to be returned to their “lawful claimants”, in an apparent reference to the opposition. The PTI was deprived of its reserved seats in the 2024 elections following the revocation of its electoral symbol. Although an SC bench declared the PTI eligible for the seats, the order was not implemented and later overturned by the constitutional bench created via the 26th Amendment, which handed them to the coalition parties that challenged the 2024 ruling. “The government cannot continue exercising parliamentary authority derived from a process that the governing coalition’s own leadership has now publicly called into question,” Tuesday’s letter read. “These seats must be restored to their rightful claimants through the appropriate legal and constitutional mechanism,” it added. The letter noted that Bilawal “described the way the opposition was stripped of its reserved seats as ‘a joke’ and said the treasury benches had simply put those seats ‘in their pockets’”. “Most damning of all, he accused the ruling government of amending the Constitution using seats that are ‘not yours’,” the document added. The signatories pointed out that these words came “from the government’s key coalition partner whose votes were required to pass both the 26th and 27th Amendments”. It continued: “The treasury benches face a question they can no longer evade. Their own coalition partner says reserved seats were taken by parties that had no right to them. “On what constitutional, legal or moral basis does the government then keep claiming the numbers through which the 26th and 27th Amendments were passed?” The lawyers and activists noted that a two-thirds majority was the safeguard the Constitution demands so that “it cannot be changed without the genuine and lawful representation of the people’s will”. However, a majority “made up with seats that were unjustly denied to the opposition is not the majority the Constitution demands”, they contended. “An amendment passed on that basis holds no constitutional, legal, or democratic validity. An amendment passed without a legitimate two-thirds majority is void from its very inception,” the letter asserted. It further said that these questions applied directly to the FCC, which “owes its existence wholly to the 27th Amendment”. “Its jurisdiction, its composition and its authority all come from a constitutional change whose legitimacy is now openly repudiated by the very people who brought it into being. “A court cannot rise higher than its source. An institution whose authors cannot defend how it was built has no foundation left to stand on,” the lawyer said. “Pakistan has witnessed far too many admissions of wrongdoing that have led to no consequences,” the letter observed, noting that leaders acknowledge violations at press conferences, express reservations, and then “allow the very arrangements they condemn to continue unchanged”. “This cycle must end. The question is no longer simply whether a wrong was committed, but whether consequences and meaningful action will follow.” The signatories stressed this was a “moment to begin repairing the grave damage caused to the judiciary and the constitutional order”. “Those in power have a choice. They can either continue to cling to an illegitimate majority or they can correct course.” The signatories include former Sindh High Court Bar Association president Salahuddin Ahmed, ex-minister Shireen Mazari, ex-senator Afrasiab Khattak, ex-MNA Bushra Gohar, HRCP Chairperson Nasir Zaidi and economist Dr Kaiser Bengali. The lawyers include Rida Hosain, Hassan Abdullah Niazi, Asad Rahim Khan, Abdul Moiz Jaferii, Khadija Siddiqi, Faisal Siddiqi, Abuzar Salman Khan Niazi and Zainab Shahid. Rights activists, including Nighat Dad and Usama Khilji, and members of the Women’s Action Forum (WAF) were among other signatories.

items.title: Centre de radiothérapie du CHU de Pala : Plus de 130 patients déjà pris en charge en sept mois
items.description: Inauguré le 24 décembre 2025 par le Président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le centre de radiothérapie du Centre hospitalier universitaire (CHU) de Pala, à Bobo-Dioulasso, affiche déjà des résultats encourageants dans la prise en charge des cancers et des tumeurs. Depuis le début de ses activités, le 13 avril 2026, l’établissement a accueilli et traité 130 patients, avec une fréquentation quotidienne estimée entre 25 et 30 malades. Onze mois après son inauguration, cette infrastructure sanitaire constitue une véritable bouffée d’oxygène pour les populations de Bobo-Dioulasso et des localités environnantes. Doté d’équipements de pointe, notamment des accélérateurs linéaires, un service de curiethérapie et un scanner de simulation, le centre contribue à améliorer significativement l’accès aux soins spécialisés en oncologie. Le centre est doté de matériels médico-techniques à la pointe de la technologie Selon le Dr Pawentaoré Esdras Zongo, médecin oncologue radiothérapeute et chef du service de radiothérapie du CHU de Pala, le centre assure la prise en charge de différentes formes de cancers, indépendamment de leur localisation et de l’âge des patients. Les cancers du sein, du col de l’utérus, de la sphère ORL et du système digestif figurent parmi les pathologies traitées. Les cancers pédiatriques sont également concernés. « Nous prenons en charge toutes les localisations et quel que soit l’âge, on peut traiter ici à Bobo, au niveau du centre de radiothérapie de Pala », a précisé le spécialiste à des hommes et femmes de médias venus visite l'infrastructure ce mardi 24 novembre 2026. Au-delà de l'offre de soins, l'ouverture de cette structure contribue à réduire les déplacements des patients vers Ouagadougou. Avant sa mise en service, de nombreux malades de la région du Guiriko et des régions voisines étaient contraints de se rendre au centre de radiothérapie de Bogodogo, dans la capitale, pour bénéficier de traitements spécialisés. Désormais, ils peuvent accéder à ces soins à Bobo-Dioulasso, du lundi au vendredi. Et, à en croire l’oncologue, le centre accueille même des patients venus de pays voisins. « Nous avons déjà traité plus d'une dizaine de malades venant du Mali », révèle le Dr Zongo, soulignant la collaboration avec les confrères maliens pour assurer leur prise en charge. Dr Pawentaoré Esdras Zongo, Chef de service radiothérapie du CHU de Pala Les premiers résultats sont également encourageants sur le plan thérapeutique. D'après le chef du service de radiothérapie, plusieurs patients ayant achevé leur traitement sont aujourd'hui en rémission ou déclarés guéris. Ils bénéficient d'un suivi médical régulier, avec des consultations de contrôle tous les trois mois, afin de surveiller leur évolution et de s'assurer de l'efficacité des traitements. Parallèlement aux soins, le centre s'investit dans la prévention et la sensibilisation. Dans le cadre des activités de communication sanitaire en langues nationales, des campagnes ont notamment été organisées autour des cancers gynécologiques et mammaires, avec un accent particulier sur le dépistage du cancer du sein et du col de l'utérus. Le mois de novembre a, quant à lui, été consacré à la sensibilisation sur le cancer de la prostate, selon le médecin. À cet effet, les hommes âgés de 50 ans et plus ont été notamment encouragés à effectuer un dépistage afin de favoriser une détection précoce de la maladie. Dr Zongo expliquant l'utilité des machines Pour toucher efficacement les populations, les équipes sanitaires privilégient, à en croire Dr Zongo, les langues nationales particulièrement utilisé, aux côtés du mooré, aussi bien lors des campagnes de sensibilisation que dans les échanges quotidiens avec les patients. « Nous utilisons ces langues pour leur expliquer leur maladie, le déroulement du traitement et les attitudes à adopter en cas d'effets secondaires » , a-t-il expliqué. Une vue de lexterieur du centre Avec ces premiers résultats, le centre de radiothérapie du CHU de Pala s'affirme donc progressivement comme un maillon important de l'offre de soins spécialisés au Burkina Faso. Oumarou KONATE Minute.bf
