items.title: 72 heures de l’Assurance 2026 : L’APSAB outille les journalistes sur les enjeux de l’assurance vie
items.description: Dans le cadre des 72 heures de l’assurance 2026, l’Association professionnelle des sociétés d’assurance du Burkina (APSAB) a organisé, ce 23 novembre à Ouagadougou, une session de formation à l’intention des journalistes. Cette initiative vise à renforcer leurs connaissances sur l’assurance vie et à faire des médias des relais d’une information plus accessible aux populations. Prévoir les imprévus, préparer sa retraite et assurer l’avenir de ses proches. L’assurance vie offre plusieurs possibilités de protection financière. Pourtant, ses mécanismes et ses avantages restent encore méconnus d’une partie de la population. C’est pour contribuer à une meilleure compréhension de cette branche que l’APSAB a réuni des professionnels des médias autour d’une session de formation, ce lundi 23 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Pour Marie Batiénon, directrice générale adjointe de UAB Assurance Vie, vice-présidente de l’APSAB et superviseure de la commission technique vie, cette initiative répond à un déficit de connaissance constaté auprès des populations. Elle estime que de nombreux Burkinabè ne maîtrisent pas encore suffisamment les principes de l’assurance, particulièrement ceux de l’assurance vie. « C’est de notre responsabilité de sensibiliser nos frères et sœurs et c’est cette dynamique que nous avons voulu enclencher en organisant cette session de formation », a-t-elle expliqué. Cette démarche s’inscrit dans une stratégie de sensibilisation plus large. Elle prévoit notamment des interventions sur les plateaux médiatiques pour mieux informer les citoyens. À l’ouverture des travaux, la responsable a également souligné la portée sociale de l’assurance vie. Elle a plaidé pour une meilleure appropriation de cet outil par les populations. « L’assurance vie devrait être comprise par tous et adoptée par tous. C’est un acte d’amour envers ceux qu’on aime et envers soi-même » , a-t-elle déclaré. Elle a, dans ce sens, invité les journalistes à contribuer à sa vulgarisation auprès du public. L’assurance vie, un levier de protection et de financement La session technique a été animée par Clément Sanwidi, directeur général de Coris Assurance Vie. Son intervention a notamment permis de mettre en lumière la contribution de l’assurance vie au développement économique. À travers la collecte de l’épargne, les compagnies d’assurance mobilisent des ressources susceptibles de participer au financement de l’économie nationale. Pour les souscripteurs, cette branche présente également plusieurs avantages. Selon le formateur, elle permet d’anticiper les besoins liés à la retraite, de constituer une épargne destinée aux études des enfants et de préserver la sécurité financière de la famille. Elle prévoit aussi des garanties en cas de décès ou d’invalidité absolue et définitive. Évoquant le rapport des Burkinabè à l’assurance, Clément Sanwidi relève un intérêt des populations pour ce secteur. Il estime toutefois que cet intérêt gagnerait à se traduire par une adhésion plus importante. Pour lui, les médias constituent des partenaires essentiels pour faire connaître les différentes offres et les garanties proposées par les sociétés d’assurance. Du côté des participants, les échanges ont permis de mieux cerner les implications de l’assurance vie. Jean-François Somé, journaliste à Minute.bf, retient particulièrement son rôle dans la préparation de l’avenir des enfants et la protection des familles. Il a également relevé la persistance de certains préjugés. Parmi eux, l’idée que l’assurance serait un service essentiellement destiné aux personnes nanties. « Au sortir de cette formation, nous sommes outillés et, en tant qu’hommes de médias, nous sommes prêts à relayer l’information juste auprès de nos populations afin de sensibiliser et aussi mobiliser, encourager les personnes à se faire assurer » , a-t-il affirmé. Cette rencontre a également marqué le lancement des activités des 72 heures de l’assurance 2026. Elle s’est achevée par une remise symbolique d’attestations de participation aux journalistes. Selon Marie Batiénon, le programme se poursuivra avec des émissions radiophoniques et télévisuelles, une conférence de presse ainsi que d’autres activités de sensibilisation. Un gala est également prévu pour marquer la clôture de cette édition. À travers ces différentes initiatives, l’APSAB entend contribuer à une meilleure connaissance de l’assurance et encourager les populations à s’intéresser davantage aux solutions de protection qu’elle propose. Éléonore Savadogo Faso7 L’article 72 heures de l’Assurance 2026 : L’APSAB outille les journalistes sur les enjeux de l’assurance vie est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Burkina Faso : Orange Burkina récompense les lauréats de l’Orange Summer Challenge (OSC) 2026
items.description: L'édition 2026 de l’Orange Summer Challenge (OSC) a connu son apothéose, ce 19 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. La cérémonie a été marquée par la remise des prix aux membres de quatre équipes porteuses de projets innovants et structurels. Le premier prix de cette édition a été remporté par les porteurs du projet Vexdrone. C'est une solution d'intelligence artificielle conçue pour détecter des anomalies sur les infrastructures électriques en faisant usage de drones. Selon les concepteurs, elle est avantageuse en ce sens qu'elle va faciliter l'inspection des infrastructures électriques et permettre aux techniciens des compagnies d'électricité de réduire le temps d'inspection en cas de panne. En guise de récompense, Orange Burkina leur a offert des équipements d'une valeur de 4 millions de FCFA. « Vraiment, on se sent heureux, on se sent vraiment heureux face à une telle situation quand on regarde un peu le parcours pendant 3 mois, les difficultés qu'on a surmontées, ça fait vraiment plaisir. Mais en même temps, c'est un challenge parce que ça ne s'arrête pas là. Nous devons représenter le Burkina Faso à l'échelle internationale » , s'est réjoui Zozerigué Traoré, porte-parole de l'équipe. L'équipe de Shango, lauréate du deuxième prix a reçu des équipements d'une valeur de 3 millions FCFA. C'est un projet de détection de pannes sur les infrastructures de l'énergie solaire. Les lauréats du troisième prix reçoivent un chèque de 2,5 millions FCFA en équipement et la quatrième équipe s'en sort avec un chèque de 2 millions de FCFA en équipement. L'édition 2026 de l'OSC s'est tenue sous le thème : « l’intelligence artificielle comme levier de croissance pour les entreprises ». Ce sont au total 200 candidatures qui ont été enregistrées. À l'issue de la phase de sélection, 20 jeunes talents ont poursuivi l'aventure pendant plusieurs semaines. Cette compétition constitue l'une des actions concrètes d'Orange Burkina en faveur de la vision du Burkina Faso en matière de technologie. Le pays veut faire de la technologie un levier de développement capable d'apporter des réponses concrètes face aux défis actuels. La représentante de la Directrice générale d'Orange Burkina, Alimata Toure/ Yao a ajouté que cette édition s'inscrit en droite ligne de la feuille de route nationale qui fait vœu de faire de l’intelligence artificielle un outil au service des besoins des populations. « Orange a fait de l'Afrique et du Moyen-Orient l'un des moteurs de sa stratégie Trust The Future. Sur un continent dont l'âge moyen avoisine 20 ans, notre conviction est simple : la jeunesse africaine est le premier atout du continent et investir sur ses compétences est l'investissement le plus rentable qui soit pour notre pays comme pour notre entreprise », a-t-elle ajouté. Également, Orange Burkina s'est fixé pour objectif la formation de plus de 3 millions de jeunes d'ici 2030 aux métiers de l'intelligence artificielle, de la cybersécurité, du cloud ainsi que de l'entrepreneuriat numérique. L’entreprise ambitionne aussi de porter à 100 le nombre de ses Orange Digital en Afrique et au Moyen-Orient. Outre cela, en 2026, plus de 12 000 jeunes ont bénéficié des programmes gratuits. Pour la seule année 2026, près de 5 000 jeunes ont été formés et accompagnés. Présent à la cérémonie, le ministre secrétaire général de la présidence du Faso, le Pr Zakaria Soré a salué Orange Burkina pour son rôle de valorisation de la jeunesse. Il a apprécié à sa juste valeur les jeunes talents pour leur sens de la créativité et de l’innovation. Il s'est réjoui de savoir qu'ils mettent en place des projets pour relever les défis existentiels des populations et des entreprises. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : Orange Burkina récompense les lauréats de l’Orange Summer Challenge (OSC) 2026 est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: COP collapse
items.description: THE collapse of climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya recently is a stark reminder of a world disinclined to cooperate for the common good. The first climate conference to end without a deal since the 2009 Copenhagen Summit, COP31 succumbed to entrenched divisions among the delegates. The main sticking point was the phasing out of fossil fuels , which was not mentioned in the draft agreement because of pressure from the petro-states including Saudi Arabia and Russia. This omission was rejected by the EU, Britain, and some small, climate-vulnerable states, which rightly hold fossil fuels responsible for global warming. Another stumbling block was the lack of commitment to providing climate finance. Ironically, many of the countries that opposed the deal for not including the transition away from fossil fuels, refused to move forward on earlier pledges to provide and mobilise funding for poor climate-vulnerable countries. It has been noted, in fact, that many of the latter prefer funds over curbs on fossil fuels at this stage, given their need to rehabilitate lives already impacted by climate change and build infrastructure strong enough to withstand future shocks. This may have been one reason why some vulnerable countries curtailed their objections to the draft deal. Day by day, the climate question is assuming greater urgency. Indeed, nature has been unrelenting against the backdrop of COP31. While Pakistan was largely spared the onrush of swelling rivers this year, Nepal witnessed a tragedy when a massive glacier collapse led to the flooding of vast tracts of land, killing hundreds. Heatwaves in Europe reportedly killed over 50,000 people last summer, while wildfires in Spain and France forced thousands of families from their homes. “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes […] along with devastating human impacts,” warns the UN’s main environmental agency in its latest Emissions Gap report. The need for cooperation and consensus on tackling climate change has never been greater. Luckily, the failure of COP31 does not spell the end of climate diplomacy. International regimes built over years to combat a danger that knows no borders are too far advanced to come undone because an agreement was not reached in Antalya. But time is running out. Given national interests and the nature of geopolitics, absolute consensus may be hard to forge. However, smaller regional initiatives, where countries — especially of the developing world — share green technology and other climate-friendly solutions can be pursued. These countries — which pollute the least but bear the brunt of global warming — have every right to ask for funds from the world’s chief polluters. The question is whether they have the will to safeguard their future through collective action. Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

items.title: The Best Place to Buy Face Wash and Frozen Orange Chicken
items.description: Earlier this year, when Trader Joe’s released a list of the 11 products its customers loved the most, a bright-pink tub of Brazil Nut Body Butter was featured among the potato chips and ice-cream sandwiches. The $6 moisturizing lotion was much cheaper than similar items on the market, the announcement noted. But its fans already knew that it was a close match for the popular $48 Sol de Janeiro Brazilian Bum Bum Cream. The TJ’s lotion had both a similar ingredient list and a similar scent of pistachio, salted caramel, and vanilla (if a less embarrassing name). That body butter is just one of the many TJ’s skin-care products that bear a striking resemblance to expensive cult favorites. The $10 vitamin C might stand in for SkinCeuticals’ $185 version. The TJ’s facial sunscreen rubs in as cleanly as a $38 Supergoop formulation. Just as Trader Joe’s snack fanatics have long tried to prove that the grocer uses the same manufacturers as name-brand favorites, people on beauty Subreddits are judging how closely TJ’s beauty offerings mimic the brands they’d find at Sephora. Like most grocery stores, Trader Joe’s has sold a limited selection of personal-care items for years. But more recently it has pushed further and further beyond the realm of lotion and tissues to offer skin-care products usually priced at a premium. Dermatologists and beauty publications now take TJ’s seriously as a beauty supplier; influencers (only semi-)joke that it’s “the next Sephora.” Buying Milky Hydrating Bi-Phase Face Mist from a store known for its frozen orange chicken might sound a little weird. But Trader Joe’s was built on what the beauty world calls “dupes,” which, in recent years, beauty consumers have become more primed to accept. Since opening its first store in the 1960s, the grocer has perfected this strategy for food. Its aisles are full of products that might remind you of other ones—instead of Oreos, they have Joe-Joe’s; instead of Swedish Fish, they have Scandinavian Swimmers. By outsourcing manufacturing to third parties, then selling the products under its private label, Trader Joe’s can undercut the competition on price. The company declined to provide details on its beauty-manufacturing process, but many beauty companies similarly use contract manufacturers, Alexis Wolfer, a McKinsey partner who’s the head of its North American beauty practice, told me. And over the past five years, those manufacturers have started “giving new or mass brands access to a lot of very similar advanced formulations that once belonged exclusively to the big houses,” she said. They’ve effectively democratized the supply chain to keep up with consumer demand for cheap, high-quality products—in effect matching what Trader Joe’s has been able to do for years with its food offerings. In some cases, Trader Joe’s and other skin-care-dupe companies can offer lower prices largely because another company already invested funds into developing the formula, Kelly Dobos, a cosmetic chemist at the University of Cincinnati, told me. About a year after the patent expired on SkinCeuticals’ original C E Ferulic serum—which pioneered a way to stabilize vitamin C, a notoriously fickle cosmetic ingredient—Trader Joe’s launched a similar formulation for $10. A leader of TJ’s beauty and health division said on the company’s podcast that she got the idea to carry a gel moisturizer after trying an expensive name-brand one. She asked one of the company’s suppliers to formulate something similar for cheaper and eventually got the $9 Ultra Hydrating Gel Moisturizer, which people now compare to a $65 formulation from Clinique. People now are also generally more willing to believe that a $10 serum can be as good as a $185 one. Dupes have been around for decades, but they took off on social media around 2022 ; by 2023, the obsession had trickled down to the mainstream enough that nearly one in three U.S. adults said they’d intentionally bought a dupe of a premium product. Just because two products have the same ingredient list doesn’t mean they’ll be equally effective, but over the years, the percentage of consumers who told McKinsey they believe that mass-beauty products can be as good as prestige ones has risen and is now at 63 percent. Whereas shoppers used to pick one price level and stick to it—your grandmother who only got her skin care at the department store, for instance—now people are more open to a good product wherever they find it. “There really isn’t the premium-beauty shopper and the mass-beauty shopper anymore,” Wolfer said. One person’s toiletry bag might contain a TJ’s cleanser they love and a $40 face mask from Sephora. Some of this price-point agnosticism is because of inflation. But people are also generally more aware of skin-care ingredients than they used to be and might be more willing to bet that Trader Joe’s $10 vitamin C serum could do its job about as well as the $185 SkinCeuticals version. That anyone who is not a dermatologist has an opinion about vitamin C serum is a sign of the “TikTok-ification of beauty,” as Wolfer put it. Beauty influencers and TikTok dermatologists, for instance, have exposed more people to Sephora “shopping haul” videos and the virtues of hyaluronic acid. And a company that wants to feed the beauty-TikTok beast can’t make just one good lotion—it has to make new ones frequently, and maybe throw in a weird ingredient people can try, like Irish sea moss, for good measure. Trader Joe’s is already set up to meet such a constant demand for new stuff (and it does carry a night cream that contains Irish-sea-moss extract). The store’s product lineup changes every week, as new products are introduced, Nakia Rohde, a Trader Joe’s spokesperson, told me. That means that the beauty aisle changes a lot as well, gaining at least one new product in October and two so far this month. Each new item doesn’t have to be terribly different from its predecessors—I doubt the company had to go back to the drawing board for its Cinnamon Roll Flavored Lip Mask after launching a vanilla-flavored one. But when one item has run its course on social media and in people’s medicine cabinets, Trader Joe’s is ready to push another on shoppers (most recently, the Espresso & Cream Flavored Lip Mask). “That also means they’ll just cut a product” out of the blue, Mark Gardiner, the author of Build a Brand Like Trader Joe’s , told me—which can motivate shoppers to pick up an extra bottle of that Supergoop-esque sunscreen, in case it’s not there the next time they visit. How someone feels about their lip mask or sunscreen—or any product, really—may depend on how much they enjoyed the shopping experience. You could purchase essentially the same body butter at CVS or Sephora or Bloomingdale’s and come away with a very different impression of how much you’d treated yourself. Trader Joe’s has spent decades figuring out how to create the illusion for budget shoppers that they are not budget shopping, Claus Ebster, a marketer who has studied Trader Joe’s, told me. With its Tiki decor, Hawaiian shirts, and vaguely flirtatious cashiers, Trader Joe’s has a more enjoyable vibe than one might expect from a store known for selling a selection of wines for $5 or less. Its store-brand product names, too, try just a little harder than they need to: Midsummer Night’s Cream has a je ne sais quoi to which the Kirkland Signature Body Lotion can only aspire. All of this can create a halo effect around Trader Joe’s products, Gardiner told me. That positive predisposition can be especially important in beauty, when a customer needs to trust a company enough to slather its product on their face. Trader Joe’s didn’t provide me with beauty-product sales figures, but the virality of some of these items suggest that at least some people are buying in. Beyond offering similar ingredients, so much of a dupe’s value comes from how well it can replicate the texture, smell, and packaging of a luxury product. But for many younger beauty shoppers, simply being able to own a bunch of products counts as a luxury, Wolfer said. Many women now show off their Trader Joe’s hauls on social media as if they’re Sephora products worth hundreds of dollars. And ultimately, this serves TJ’s well: People seeking luxury-ish moisturizer on a tight budget will have one more reason to come to the store, and maybe pick up a frozen pizza from Italy along with a cheap bottle of wine for a nice night in. No one’s fooling themselves that this is the exact equivalent of ordering a pizza made with D.O.P. mozzarella di Bufala , opening a bottle of Greco di Tufo, and doing a home facial with $800 of La Mer products. But for many people, it’s close enough.

items.title: Yélimané : Gory fait le point sur la gestion du fonds minier et de la TDRL

items.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill 7, including senior security official
items.description: Israeli airstrikes in Gaza on Tuesday killed seven people, including Hamas’s director of internal security, Palestinian officials in the territory told AFP, despite a ceasefire in place since last year. Israel’s military said it had struck a senior Hamas official. Gaza’s interior ministry said an airstrike in Gaza City killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahal, director-general of the Internal Security Service. Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza’s civil defence agency, told AFP that several other people were in critical condition following the same strike in Gaza City’s Rimal neighbourhood. The strike comes as talks are underway in Israel to form a new government after October legislative elections produced no clear winner. Centrist Gadi Eisenkot wants to form a coalition to end caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure. But Netanyahu, who has staked his reputation on ensuring security for Israel after the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, remains in charge of military operations while negotiations continue. Police station strike Bassal said earlier on Tuesday that three people, including a 17-year-old, had been killed in a separate Israeli airstrike near Gaza City. Three more were also killed in a third airstrike on a police station in the Al-Mawasi area in southern Gaza, he added. Gaza’s police force said two policemen aged 23 and 33 were among the dead. It condemned the strike as “part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus”. Israel’s military said it “struck terrorists in the area” of the police station, but did not confirm the strike that killed the 17-year-old. Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of war triggered by the October 2023 attack. More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the truce, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry. In the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers have been killed, as well as one civilian contractor. Most of Gaza’s population of 2.1 million live displaced in tents or makeshift shelters in the territory, where Israel’s military says it controls more than 60 per cent of the land.

items.title: Justice sportive mondiale : Kéba Mbaye, le Sénégalais qui a donné naissance au TAS
items.description: À l'heure où le Sénégal se retrouve devant le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) dans son bras de fer avec le Maroc, un pan méconnu de l'histoire de cette juridiction mérite d'être rappelé. Cette institution, devenue incontournable dans le règlement des litiges sportifs internationaux, porte une empreinte sénégalaise considérable. Son histoire est intimement liée à un magistrat d'exception : Kéba Mbaye. L'idée initiale revient à Juan Antonio Samaranch, président du Comité international olympique (CIO) à partir de 1980. Mais entre concevoir une idée et lui donner une existence juridique et institutionnelle, il y a un travail considérable. C'est précisément dans cette étape décisive que le Sénégalais Kéba Mbaye a joué un rôle déterminant. En 1982, le CIO constitue un groupe de travail chargé de mettre en place cette nouvelle juridiction. À sa tête, Kéba Mbaye, alors magistrat à la Cour internationale de justice et membre du mouvement olympique. Sa mission consiste à traduire le projet de Samaranch en une institution opérationnelle, dotée de règles et de statuts. Sous sa conduite, les fondements juridiques du futur tribunal sont élaborés. Les premiers statuts sont ratifiés en 1983. Le 30 juin 1984, le TAS devient officiellement opérationnel. Kéba Mbaye en devient le premier président. Son rôle ne s'arrête pas à cette naissance institutionnelle. Il dirige le tribunal pendant plus de vingt ans, jusqu'à son décès en janvier 2007, accompagnant son développement et son affirmation progressive dans le paysage sportif international. En 1984, il publie également dans l'Annuaire français de droit international un article consacré à cette nouvelle institution d'arbitrage. Une contribution qui témoigne de son implication intellectuelle dans la conception de cette juridiction. Le parcours de Kéba Mbaye éclaire la confiance placée en lui. Ancien premier président de la Cour suprême du Sénégal et vice-président de la Cour internationale de justice à La Haye de 1981 à 1990, il était l'un des juristes africains les plus respectés de son époque. Son expertise a été déterminante pour donner au TAS ses fondements et sa crédibilité juridique. L'institution a certes évolué depuis sa création. En 1994, une réforme conduit à la mise en place du Conseil international de l'arbitrage en matière de sport (CIAS), chargé notamment de garantir l'indépendance du TAS vis-à-vis du CIO. Mais cette évolution n'efface en rien l'héritage de son premier architecte. Quarante-deux ans après ses débuts, le TAS est devenu une référence mondiale, appelé à trancher les contentieux les plus sensibles du sport, du dopage aux sanctions disciplinaires, en passant par les litiges contractuels et les conflits entre fédérations. Dans le contexte du différend Sénégal-Maroc, cette histoire prend une résonance particulière. Le Sénégal défend aujourd'hui ses intérêts devant une juridiction dont l'un des principaux bâtisseurs fut un de ses illustres fils. Ce rappel historique ne constitue évidemment ni un argument juridique ni une garantie sur l'issue du dossier. Il souligne cependant la contribution remarquable d'un Sénégalais à la construction d'une institution qui occupe désormais une place centrale dans la gouvernance du sport mondial. Le TAS n'est pas une création exclusivement sénégalaise. Mais dans sa conception juridique, sa mise en place et ses premières années de fonctionnement, l’empreinte de Kéba Mbaye est si profonde qu'elle mérite d'être pleinement reconnue. Le Sénégal peut légitimement s'enorgueillir d'avoir contribué, à travers l'un de ses plus illustres magistrats, à bâtir l'une des institutions majeures de la justice sportive internationale. Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: CRADAT : Ramatoulaye Camara lance les travaux des experts en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration
items.description: La Guinée renoue avec les sessions ordinaires du Centre régional africain de l’administration du travail (CRADAT), après près de trois décennies d’absence. La ministre guinéenne de l’Emploi, du Travail et de la Protection sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara, a donné, ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, le coup d’envoi des travaux des experts, en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration de l’institution. La cérémonie s’est déroulée à Conakry, en présence de son homologue sénégalais de la Fonction et du Travail, ainsi que du directeur général du CRADAT, Arsène Armand Hien. Cette rencontre technique constitue une étape importante dans la préparation de la session ministérielle prévue jeudi prochain. Elle permettra aux experts d’examiner les conclusions de la précédente session extraordinaire, de vérifier la conformité des décisions et recommandations adoptées et de préparer un rapport destiné aux ministres. Dans son allocution d’ouverture, la ministre Ramatoulaye Camara a souhaité la bienvenue aux délégations présentes en Guinée, qu’elle a présentée comme une terre d’hospitalité, de richesse et d’innovation, ouverte au monde. « Au nom de Son Excellence Monsieur le Président de la République, Monsieur Mamadi Doumbouya, et au nom du Chef du gouvernement, Monsieur Amadou Oury Bah, je voudrais vous exprimer toute notre satisfaction de vous accueillir à Conakry », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre a également souligné le caractère particulier de cette rencontre, rappelant que la Guinée n’avait plus accueilli cette importante activité depuis 1997. Elle a invité les participants à mettre leur expertise au service de l’institution, en misant sur la qualité des échanges et la pertinence des recommandations qui seront soumises aux ministres. « Je compte, nous comptons donc sur l'expertise de tous, sur la qualité des échanges et la pertinence de vos recommandations pour contribuer au rayonnement de notre institution commune », a-t-elle insisté. Au-delà des travaux, la ministre a exprimé le souhait de voir les délégations découvrir les réalités et les ambitions de la Guinée, notamment à travers son programme de développement socio-économique et durable, Simandou 2040. Prenant la parole à son tour, le directeur général du CRADAT, Arsène Armand Hien, s’est réjoui du retour de l’institution à Conakry après 29 ans d’absence. Il a qualifié cette rencontre d’historique, soulignant le rôle joué par la Guinée dans la relance des sessions ordinaires du Conseil d’administration. « Le CRADAT est heureux que ça soit la Guinée qui a remis sur les rails la session ordinaire. C'est bon de le préciser et de le relever », a-t-il affirmé. Selon lui, les experts auront pour mission de reprendre le rapport de la session extraordinaire afin de s’assurer que les décisions et recommandations retenues sont conformes aux conclusions précédemment arrêtées. Le rapport issu de ces travaux sera ensuite transmis à la session ministérielle, qui se tiendra jeudi. Le directeur général a salué l’engagement de la Guinée, dont l’accueil marque une nouvelle étape dans le fonctionnement de cette institution régionale. Le ministre sénégalais de la Fonction et du Travail a, pour sa part, exprimé sa satisfaction de prendre part à cette rencontre à Conakry. Il a salué l’accueil réservé à sa délégation et remercié son homologue guinéenne pour les dispositions prises en vue de leur séjour. Évoquant les relations professionnelles déjà nouées entre les deux pays, il a rappelé les échanges antérieurs entre le Conseil du dialogue social du Sénégal et le Conseil national du dialogue social (CNDS) de Guinée. Le ministre sénégalais a également insisté sur l’importance du CRADAT dans l’évolution des administrations du travail en Afrique. « Je crois qu'aujourd'hui un centre d'une importance capitale que constitue donc le CRADAT a besoin quand même d'aller vers la modernisation de l'administration du travail », a-t-il souligné. Tout en saluant le travail accompli par le directeur général et son équipe, il a exprimé sa confiance dans la capacité des experts à produire un rapport de qualité, susceptible de faciliter les travaux de la session ministérielle. La tenue de cette 45e session ordinaire à Conakry intervient ainsi dans un contexte marqué par la volonté des États membres de renforcer la coopération régionale et de promouvoir une administration du travail plus moderne, efficace et adaptée aux défis du continent. Youssouf Keita L’article CRADAT : Ramatoulaye Camara lance les travaux des experts en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: 'Watching me with eyes of fire': Pope Francis revealed in personal diary having seen devil
items.description: The late Pope Francis recounted seeing the devil three times and, on one occasion, the “gate of hell”, in excerpts from his personal diary published on Tuesday in a new book. The Private Diary of Pope Francis , by Argentine Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernandez, includes passages taken from a journal the former Jorge Bergoglio kept between 1992 and 2024, a document that reveals his worries, regrets and self-critiques — as well as his enormous humanity and faith. Fernandez, head of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, said he was asked by Francis to help make known to the world the musings inside the black plastic journal. Upon Francis’s death last year, Fernandez expressed concern to his successor, Leo XIV, that the book “might end up abandoned in a warehouse somewhere”. He was allowed to publish passages, noting that “the spiritual concerns present in his heart are very explicit and can be helpful to us”. In one of the most intriguing revelations, Francis writes that while archbishop of Buenos Aires, he saw the devil three different times including “from the car when I was returning to the house, and in the choir loft during Mass” and once in Rome following a visit to Chile. “I discovered that the devil had been brazenly lurking around cunningly,” wrote Francis in his journal on January 24, 2021, according to a copy of the English language version of the book published by Penguin Random House and viewed by AFP . Francis wrote that he recalled three episodes “when I don’t doubt he was physically present”. “More or less fifteen years ago. I saw him from the car window. I can’t forget his menacing and, at the same time, seductive eyes,” he wrote. During the second episode inside a Carmelite chapel, Francis wrote: “He was watching me with eyes of fire”. “I can’t forget that gaze, stronger than the previous. They were like flames of fire.” The third episode occurred during a meeting in Rome, following a visit to Chile. “I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything… I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice,” he wrote, adding that “the Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me”. Francis also revealed, on June 7, 2018, that on the night before, while getting ready to go to sleep, he “saw the entrance to hell”. “Pagan seduction in full force. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me,” he said, adding that he “grabbed the Rosary as a weapon”. “It’s dangerous to approach the gate of hell because flames can leap out and burn,” he wrote. Self critiques Throughout the diary, Francis does not hesitate to criticise himself, for his occasional “feelings of disdain, envy, pride” or for having ignored a drunk man in the street who addressed him “because I wanted to have a serene walk”. “The proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge” is how the former pope described himself on December 30, 2022. On January 15, 2017, he confessed that for a few days he had been experiencing “a very bad spirit of anger and discontent”. While charismatic, Pope Francis also had a strong personality and was sometimes criticised within the Curia, the Catholic Church’s governing body, for being authoritarian. Mercy is a recurrent theme in the journal. “I felt, looking back, all the evil I’ve done in life. I’m in such abundant need of the Lord’s mercy!” he wrote on January 5, 1997. End of life Pope Francis appeared to worry that his days on Earth would be short-lived, fretting over his ageing and the need to “bear it”. In 1996, at age 60 — nearly three decades before his death — he wrote: “I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good. “How much time I’ve used badly! How much badly done!” In 2001, he wrote that “these 65 years make me think about the end. I’m already counting down”. The worries continued even after becoming pope in 2013, with Francis writing on April 9, 2016 that “the attacks of the devil under different aspects have increased… Could it be a sign that my time is up and he doesn’t want to lose?” The journal contains 86 pages written before his election as pope in 2013, and another 55 written afterwards. One of the briefest — and most moving — passages in Francis’s diary comes on July 21, 2013: “On March 13, they elected me pope.” Francis died on April 21, 2025.

items.title: Relief orgs assess humanitarian needs in Mershing, South Darfur
items.description: A delegation representing eight UN agencies and international humanitarian organisations has visited Mershing locality in South Darfur to assess living conditions and the needs of local communities following what local authorities describe as one of the worst agricultural seasons in the area’s history. Farmers and pastoralists are among those most affected by the deteriorating situation. The delegation comprises the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and five international organisations: ZOA, World Vision, Mercy Corps, LM International, and NIDDO. Mershing locality executive director Oqba Abdelhamid told Radio Dabanga that the visit was intended to assess the humanitarian conditions facing residents, particularly farmers and pastoralists, following the deterioration of the agricultural season. He said the delegation had held direct meetings with residents in Manawashi to hear their complaints and observations and identify their actual needs. The programme also includes field visits to assess essential social services, including water, healthcare, and education, and to hear from different sections of the local community ahead of determining the humanitarian interventions required. Abdelhamid said the visit would continue to the town of Mershing on Tuesday before extending to El Malam locality. He expressed hope that these efforts would help ease residents’ suffering and improve the humanitarian response to their needs. items.title: TPI de Siguiri : 11 femmes, dont des Sierra-Léonaises, condamnées pour exploitation illégale de l’or et dégradation de l’environnement
items.description: Le verdict est tombé ce lundi 23 novembre 2026 au tribunal de première instance (TPI) de Siguiri. Onze femmes, dont des Sierra-Léonaises, poursuivies pour exploitation illégale de l’or et dégradation de l’environnement, ont été condamnées. Chacune a écopé d’un an d’emprisonnement assorti de sursis et du paiement d’une amende de 3 millions de francs guinéens. Interpellées le 17 novembre dernier dans différentes zones minières, ces prévenues avaient été placées en détention à la maison d’arrêt de Siguiri, dans le cadre des mesures préventives prises par les autorités pour mettre fin à l’exploitation artisanale de l’or sur les sites concernés de la région administrative de Siguiri. Lors de leur comparution devant le juge audiencier, ces onze femmes ont toutes reconnu les faits qui leur sont reprochés. Au cours des débats, certaines ont évoqué leur statut de veuves et expliqué que l’exploitation minière constituait pour elles un moyen de subvenir aux besoins alimentaires de leurs enfants et de leurs familles. D’autres ont également mis en avant les difficultés financières et la précarité dans lesquelles elles vivent. Dans ses réquisitions, le ministère public, représenté par le substitut du procureur de la République près le tribunal de première instance de Siguiri, Simon Pierre Milimono, a demandé au tribunal de retenir ces femmes dans les liens de la prévention et de les condamner à deux ans d’emprisonnement assortis de sursis et au paiement d’une amende de 3 millions de francs guinéens chacune. Après examen du dossier et des débats à l’audience, le tribunal, présidé par Aboubacar 3 Barry, a finalement prononcé contre chacune des onze femmes une peine d’un an d’emprisonnement avec sursis, assortie du paiement d’une amende de 3 millions de francs guinéens. Nouhan Konaté, correspondant régional basé à Siguiri L’article TPI de Siguiri : 11 femmes, dont des Sierra-Léonaises, condamnées pour exploitation illégale de l’or et dégradation de l’environnement est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Freedom of speech should not become a shield for those crossing 'red lines', says Naqvi
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Tuesday asserted that freedom of speech should not become a shield for those who cross “red lines”. He made the remarks while addressing a seminar organised by the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI). At the outset of his speech, the minister said that there were four “red lines” for the state: terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence and sexual exploitation of children. “On these four points, there is no compromise. Pakistan has paid for terrorism in blood. As interior minister, I have attended the funerals of martyrs. And very often, the hate that killed them began on a mobile phone,” he said. He alleged that only 47 per cent of the complaints made by the Counter Terrorism Department were acted upon by social media platforms. “This is not about technology, this is about people. We are not saying that free speech must be curtailed […] journalists must report, citizens must question, dissent must be heard, including against the government, but freedom of speech can never become a shield for those who cross these red lines,” he said. He went on to say that Pakistan had “limited manpower”, resources and technology. Giving the example of Punjab, he said that the province had a population of 140 million against a strength of 61 people in the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA). “And these 61 people include drivers, clerks and officers. We cannot do this alone. That is why we have established a Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority,” he said. The minister called for moving from policy towards enforcement. “To begin with [social media] platforms, OTT services and major content creators must register with the authority. Registration is not a licence to silence anyone, it tells us who is accountable when something goes wrong,” he said. He said that every social media platform “must name an empowered representative for Pakistan, who can actually take decisions”. “Similarly, citizens need one complaint channel they can track. We are moving all NCCIA complaints onto the Pak ID app and the authority is building a single fully tracked complaint system,” he said. Naqvi then went on to recount a recent town hall meeting, where he met five girls who were on the verge of ending their lives due to someone about to release “sensitive material” on social media platforms. “We don’t have any pathway for approaching those platforms. It’s their responsibility to react immediately to save these innocent lives,” he said. The minister said that the social media authority would verify whether action had been taken or not. “Finally, enforcement will be step by step: engagement, then notice, then penalties. Blocking a whole [social media] platform will remain a last resort … our request will be clear, lawful and open to review,” he said. “The state should not feel helpless. Yet, we see terrorist groups still recruiting, still raising terrorist funds, still spreading fear on these very platforms,” he said. Giving an example, Naqvi said that the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) was a declared terrorist organisation, yet “many of their officials are still using these platforms”. “If it is a declared [terrorist] organisation, then who allows them to move around and use all these platforms? Someone needs to stop [them]. This is our request,” he said. “If you are not doing it, what meaning should we take? If it is declared by your country that this organisation is a blacklisted organisation, is a terrorist organisation and then you don’t take action, there’s a big question mark,” he said. He added that the government was focusing on the capacity building of the NCCIA. “Today, I extend an open hand to all these platforms. Let us sit together, not across the table. Operate globally, be accountable globally and never let Pakistani citizens feel unheard,” he concluded.

items.description: When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrived and left the Apec host city Shenzhen last week, retired diplomat Zhang Qiyue was there on the red carpet for the greeting and send-off. items.title: Gaza : la méningite gagne du terrain dans des conditions sanitaires alarmantes
items.description: L’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) tire la sonnette d’alarme face à une forte hausse des cas de méningite dans la bande de Gaza depuis la mi-octobre. Plus de 530 cas ont été recensés, dont une majorité chez les très jeunes enfants. L’agence onusienne appelle à renforcer d’urgence l’approvisionnement en fournitures médicales et en équipements de laboratoire pour améliorer le dépistage et la prise en charge des malades.

items.title: Féminicides : chaque heure, 5 femmes dans le monde tuées par leur conjoint ou un parent
items.description: Environ 47 000 femmes et filles ont été tuées en 2025 par leur partenaire ou un membre de leur famille, selon de nouvelles données rendues public par l'ONU. Alors que les féminicides reculent moins vite que les autres homicides, les victimes de violences sont de moins en moins nombreuses à demander de l’aide, faute de confiance dans les institutions censées les protéger.

items.title: The Big Bang Theory : A Theory
items.description: Sheldon Cooper would want to begin with the numbers, so here they are: In 2026, Americans have spent more than 27.5 billion minutes watching the CBS sitcom he anchors, The Big Bang Theory —making it the year’s most popular streaming show among U.S. adults. (Its only rival? The cartoon Bluey , beloved by kids and grown-ups.) Per numbers gathered by Nielsen and aggregated by the data journalist Daniel Parris, Big Bang has surpassed the viewership of a host of newer and buzzier programs, among them The Pitt , Bridgerton , and Stranger Things —this despite the fact that the series premiered nearly 20 years ago and ended its network run in 2019. The show’s current success, Sheldon might observe, is not a statistical anomaly. On the contrary, the series has regularly featured in Nielsen’s Top 10 streaming rankings for the past three years. This year, though, “the show’s viewership has surged to an all-time high,” Parris noted recently in his Stat Significant newsletter. No bombshell from Love Island USA , it seems, can compete with the charms of a theoretical physicist who has an IQ of 187 and an endless desire to remind you about it. In some ways, Big Bang ’s popularity tracks: Nerds are cool now, you might have heard, and few things prove that point as eloquently as the billions of minutes Americans are spending in the geeky company of Sheldon (played by Jim Parsons), the experimental physicist Leonard Hofstadter (Johnny Galecki), the astrophysicist Rajesh Koothrappali (Kunal Nayyar), and the aerospace engineer Howard Wolowitz (Simon Helberg). In another way, though, the show’s afterlife is curious. Big Bang is notably dated, both in its storylines (see: the advent of Siri) and in its sense of humor (among other things, it has been said to have a woman problem ). And even in this Muskified moment , telegenic nerdiness is not the instant sell that Sheldon et al. might want it to be. Genius is, pretty much by definition, unrelatable. Yet the show serves up storylines about science experiments and string theory and Star Trek ’s Kobayashi Maru . Like a Comic-Con panel with plot points, it features cameos from an array of nerd-world luminaries—Stan Lee, LeVar Burton, Wil Wheaton, Neil deGrasse Tyson, and many more. You might expect a sitcom to amuse you. You might not expect it to do so through assorted jokes about Schrödinger’s cat . But Big Bang ’s singularity ( guess what the show also jokes about) helps explain how a TV series, like Schrödinger’s four-legged thought experiment, can be both long dead and very much alive. Series in motion tend to stay in motion, and Big Bang was big from the beginning: During its initial airing, it was regularly one of the most watched series on network TV. Today, it’s a well-promoted presence on HBO Max. Its scenes are repackaged on TikTok. Its spin-offs— Young Sheldon , Georgie and Mandy’s First Marriage , and Stuart Fails to Save the Universe —double, Parris notes in his analysis, as free advertising for the original show. And Big Bang , given the length of its run, is quite a lot of show: 12 seasons, at roughly 20 episodes each, amounting to—well, I’ll leave the exact math to Sheldon, but many, many hours of autoplay-friendly entertainment. The physics, though—the blunt ubiquities that keep Big Bang ever in the ether—are only part of the equation. The show is one of several vintage sitcoms, among them Friends , Seinfeld , New Girl , and The Office , that have proved steadily popular in the streaming era. They owe at least some of that success to the genre they share. Sitcoms’ most widely disparaged tendencies (predictability, low stakes, high camp) are, for many audiences, their most appealing features. Their anodyne nature offers the very thing that so many modern viewers crave: comfort TV. [ Read: Why you can’t stop streaming Seinfeld. Or Frasier. Or Bones. ] Big Bang —a show that finds Leonard, the most socially aware of the geniuses, telling a joke whose punch line is spherical chickens in a vacuum —might seem to deviate from the sitcom’s standard formulas. Instead, it takes them to their logical extremes. A gang of lovable misfits? Check: Sheldon and his friends are so thoroughly misfit that they find themselves barred from a game of Dungeons & Dragons. Plotlines that find humor in banality? Check: Big Bang devoted an episode to Howard’s engineering of a “zero-gravity waste-disposal system” for astronauts on the International Space Station. Jokes that are sharp but accessible? Check again: Here’s Raj’s reaction to Howard’s creation of an extraterrestrial toilet: “This is an important achievement for two reasons: No. 1—and, of course, No. 2.” The friends regularly tease one another; mockery, in this group, is a love language. But they also support one another, reflexively. After Howard’s space commode has been installed on the ISS, he realizes that he has made a mistake with its specs. The guys rally around him, gathering junk that mimics the equipment on the station and staying up all night to help him correct the error. The scenes that result—think Apollo 13 with pizza boxes and poop jokes—are core to Big Bang ’s appeal: Competence can be its own source of comfort. And when it’s a team effort? The comfort compounds. It’s nice to watch people being good at things. It’s even nicer to watch them being good at things while being good to one another. In this, too, Big Bang adheres to well-worn formulas. Every sitcom, whether its characters are relatives or neighbors or co-workers, will be, to some extent, a show about family. Big Bang ’s variation on the theme—genius, in loco familias —is especially poignant because the family the characters build is so unlikely. These are people who, if they hadn’t found one another, might not have anybody else. Had Friends ’ Monica and Rachel lived across the hall from two guys who weren’t Chandler and Joey, they probably would have befriended the other guys anyway: Whatever the characters’ quirks, socializing came naturally to them. Big Bang ’s foursome, though, are more than mere outliers; they’re also outcasts. The guys spent much of their childhoods being bullied. They grew up with families who may have loved them but who didn’t, and couldn’t, fully understand them. To be exceptionally smart, these characters have learned, is to be perpetually excluded. Their baseline condition is isolation. Friendship is a statistical improbability. But this bleak math, rather than compromising the show’s comforts, amplifies them. It heightens the stakes of the characters’ relationships and makes the community that they find, against the odds, all the more remarkable. The guys may sometimes annoy one another. They occasionally misunderstand one another. Yet their bonds never break. Members of the group—which, over the seasons, expands to include the microbiologist Bernadette Rostenkowski (Melissa Rauch) and the neuroscientist Amy Farrah Fowler (Mayim Bialik)—keep coming back together. And all of them keep choosing one another until, eventually, they no longer need to. The thing about chosen family is that it can keep accruing. In Big Bang ’s pilot episode, Sheldon and Leonard get a random new neighbor, an aspiring actress named Penny (Kaley Cuoco). And Penny, once dumb luck has put her in the path of these geniuses, sets several forces in motion. She is a chemical agent in the guys’ lives, fizzing and sparking and transforming everything in her path. Her influence—her kindness, her wit, her tendency to call everyone “sweetie”—transforms Sheldon and Leonard. It makes them savvier and worldlier than they were before: two men, book-smart and street-stupid, whom Penny’s influence turns wise. Insiders and outsiders, assembling and clashing and learning and growing: Writers might talk about character arcs. Scientists might talk about evolution. In his recently released memoir (titled, aptly, Sitcom ), Chuck Lorre, Big Bang ’s co-creator and executive producer, describes the show’s transformation from its initial premise ( geeks, lol ) into the one that made it to the air. Big Bang ’s early pilot, he writes, lacked depth and warmth. It lacked, crucially, Penny and Raj and Howard. It was coming along at a moment when nerds were gaining cultural cachet; rather than humanizing its geeks, though, it resorted to skewering them. Network executives hated it. But CBS gave Lorre and his co-creator, Bill Prady, an opportunity nearly unheard of in network television: a do-over. They revamped the show to feature four geniuses rather than two. They rewrote the woman-next-door character—who is smarter than she might seem, but neurotypical enough to hear “pi” and think of a baked good—as much more central to the story. The Penny who emerged was also, effectively, a stand-in for the show’s audience. Initially baffled by her wacky new neighbors, she comes to appreciate them and soon enough to love them. She encourages the show’s audience to do the same. [ Read: The (slow, awkward) love song of Sheldon Cooper ] What audiences adore is perhaps best encapsulated by a scene featured in Young Sheldon , Big Bang ’s first spin-off. The show follows Sheldon, age 10, as an up-and-coming genius living in a small town in East Texas. At one point, he is shown rigging a radio to listen to a faraway event that is, for him, the Super Bowl and the Oscars in one: the announcement of the year’s Nobel laureates, live from Stockholm. Giddy, Sheldon invites everyone he knows—his family, his academic mentors, the entire student body of his very large high school—to join him for an early-morning listening party. Nobody shows. Emotions, as Sheldon will readily admit, are not his strong suit. Still, he is crushed. The scene is hard to watch: a kid, abandoned by everyone he knows, in direct violation of the laws of comfort TV. But then the camera cuts away from Sheldon, panning out from East Texas to homes in California and India and Nebraska and to the kids who, in 1990, occupied them: Howard playing video games, Raj studying, Penny asleep in her bed. As Young Sheldon becomes, briefly, Young Howard , Young Raj , and the like—as viewers see Leonard in his room in New Jersey, riveted by the same Nobel broadcast—Diana Ross & the Supremes’ “Someday We’ll Be Together” plays in the background. The montage is treacly, sure. You might see it as evidence of corporate interests at work: an ad for the franchise’s original show, product-placed in the new one. But the scene fits. Family is, in its way, an act of vertical integration—a series of connections that can support all of the people they touch. And Young Sheldon ’s audience, for once, knows something that the genius cannot: Togetherness, for him, is a foregone conclusion. His path will lead him to his people. He is alone for now. But he won’t be for long. ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: ‘Our History Is Better Than Anybody Else’s’
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. F or years now, Donald Trump and the MAGA movement have cast the United States as the heir to and defender of Western civilization. In the second Trump administration, this sort of grandiose rhetoric has increased; the administration presents itself as the lone bulwark against the barbarians at the gates who would annihilate everything good about the world. “Our lineage and our legacy hails back to Athens, to Rome,” Stephen Miller, Trump’s longtime adviser and new chief of staff, said at the funeral for the assassinated conservative activist Charlie Kirk. “Our ancestors built the cities. They produced the art and architecture. They built the industry” that pulled “us out of the caves and the darkness into the light.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a similar speech a month ago, in actual Athens. “The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West,” Rubio announced. “This was the foundation of the Western mind: Our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the Gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom.” Certainly one can see the legacy of ancient societies in how we live today—the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle, the many denominations of Christianity descended from its embrace by the Romans, the Romance languages spoken from Santiago to Sambava. The American Founders took inspiration from antiquity, a debt you can see in the mighty structures surrounding the National Mall. Yet what many conservatives describe as Western civilization is not so much a consistent historical fact as an ideological project, one that has long been used to demonstrate the inherent superiority of certain people—white people—in order to legitimize a claim to power and dominance. Europe and the West began to emerge as coherent political identities relatively recently, in the early 17th century; they are not timeless, immutable concepts. [ Adam Serwer: The GOP’s message to immigrants ] Some conservative-media figures have been explicit about what they mean by Western civilization. The right-wing podcaster Matt Walsh described Americans as “the best innovators, lawmakers, scientists, artists, athletes, thinkers, and fighters in the entire world. We’re not a ‘melting pot’ or a mishmash of inferior, squabbling cultures.” If the country could just “evict anti-American invaders,” it could go back to being “an unstoppable force advancing the interests of civilization, without apology.” That apology is the problem: America, and by extension the West, has grown weak because it has stopped asserting its superiority over others as a means of honoring its inheritance. “Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional,” Rubio said, and that shame threatened to condemn Americans to “a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.” This sort of argument plays well at rallies, and conservatives have long been trying to institutionalize and intellectualize it through college curricula. But it is based on an outdated historiography that takes into account neither how these ancient societies saw themselves nor their relationship to the societies around them. It is a bedtime story about being the bestest boys who ever lived—in short, a myth. And at the core of this myth is the idea that human progress is the product of isolation and ethnic homogeneity, rather than a collective endeavor. It is one thing to take inspiration from past societies, and another entirely to claim their accomplishments as your own personal inheritance. This is a race-based argument, as if the accomplishment of a Caesar, an Alexander, or a Napoleon belonging to all white people carries any more weight than the average Eagles fan saying, “We won the Super Bowl.” There is no question that Greek and Roman texts from antiquity—Aristotle’s Poetics , Cicero’s speeches, Sappho’s poetry—are worthy of study. Concepts associated with Western civilization, such as democracy, freedom of speech, religious tolerance, and capitalism, have undoubtedly shaped the modern world. But appreciating the canonical texts of what Rubio and others refer to as Western civilization is not the same as telling the story they want to tell, which is that virtually every human achievement of note was attained by Europeans. T he culprit for the West’s loss of confidence, many conservatives believe, is the “woke” university. Richard Nixon said, “The professors are the enemy,” half a century ago, but educational polarization—the drift of college-educated voters to the left and non-college-educated voters to the right—has lent the critique a new urgency. The former Trump adviser Steve Bannon recently told The Boston Globe that universities were the only reason Democrats are “able to compete with us.” One response is to try to force students to learn a particular version of the story of Western civilization, a version that is not a neutral account of concepts such as capitalism, democracy, and Christianity, but an argument that capitalism, democracy, and Christianity are superior to the heathen cultures of foreign barbarians. Republican legislatures and administrators in states such as Texas and Florida have moved to reorient university curricula toward this vision. The Democrats’ sweep of state offices in Texas may halt some of these changes, but unwinding them will take time, while the general trend in red states is likely to continue. In 2023, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis championed legislation to “ensure Florida’s public universities and colleges are grounded in the history and philosophy of Western Civilization.” William Inboden, the provost at the University of Texas at Austin, has called for a renewed commitment “to the American people, our constitutional order, Western civilization, and the classical liberal arts.” The shift at UT Austin and elsewhere coincided with the slashing of courses related to race and gender—perhaps because these subjects threaten to complicate the preferred narrative of Western civilization. Conservatives have tried to present this effort as “depoliticizing” scholarship, in Inboden’s description. But historians are always making new discoveries or reinterpreting old ones. What these conservatives are really attempting to do is stop the process of revision and rediscovery in favor of past interpretations that promote the idea that America is the successor to the great civilizations of antiquity, and is thus entitled to dominate the world in the name of humanity. “One powerful tool of legitimacy is invoking a past golden age,” the historian Ada Palmer writes in Inventing the Renaissance . “Golden ages are mythical constructions (the events are real but the golden ageness is invented), so it’s easy to claim you are the true successor, even if you have little historical connection.” The question, though, is legitimacy for what? America’s Founders were arguably some of the original Roman-statue guys: Grounding American independence in the Greco-Roman world allowed the colonists to smooth over denominational divides and justify their own freedoms alongside the institution of slavery and the dispossession of Native Americans. John Stuart Mill argued that “despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement.” Convenient for the despot! What this narrative misses is the fact that the idea of separate civilizations at all is a relatively young one. In How the World Made the West , the classical historian Josephine Quinn identifies the idea as originating in the 19th century, alongside, not coincidentally, the age of colonization. European nations that sought to subjugate other peoples found it convenient to posit that those peoples were inferior, and that despotism was thus justified. The world was hardly harmonious before that; war and ethnic strife were common. But the concept of civilization was generally thought of as singular, Quinn writes, as in human civilization. The narrative of separate civilizations was later adapted for the Cold War, and revived for the post-9/11 era. Now it has been resurrected as self-soothing rhetoric for a right-wing-populist project, a kind of collectivist monarchist belief that white people—or, in euphemism, “the West”—are born to rule. But we know now that the world of antiquity was much more interconnected than was previously believed. As Quinn writes, human civilization is a story of “exchange between people from different places and cultures,” and “without it there wouldn’t be much of a story at all.” Ancient Greece took inspiration from the Egyptians to its south and the Phoenicians (from whom they drew their alphabet) and Assyrians to its east. The Iliad and The Odyssey , Quinn writes, “show us that Greek speakers of that era still chose to sing of international kingdoms, intercontinental war, and voyages across broad seas.” Greek coins and Roman amphorae have been found in India, where Alexander led his army and where Greek kingdoms existed for centuries afterward. Augustus’s legions marched south along the Nile until halted by the queen of Kush, a kingdom that had been in contact with the Greeks for generations and had provided Egypt with many of its rulers. We do math with Arabic numerals, and the concept of zero was invented by an Indian mathematician in the seventh century. The main religion of Western civilization, Christianity, was founded by an Aramaic-speaking rabbi in West Asia. Agriculture, philosophy, literacy, navigation, metalworking—all of these advanced in antiquity because goods and people traveled, and ideas traveled with them. “What are called Western values—freedom, rationality, justice, and tolerance—are not only or originally western,” Quinn writes, “and the West itself is in large part a product of long-standing links with a much larger network of societies, to south and north as well as east.” I am not arguing that these societies were “superior” to Western ones—only that societies learn from contact with one another rather than through ethnic purity and enforced segregation. Taking the Greeks and Romans as the origin of Western civilization is an ideological project, not a historical one, a little bit like a posthumous baptism. The ancients largely did not see race the way many of our contemporaries do: as an immutable biological category. Projecting that conception backwards is like imagining that Xerxes scrolled through updates on the Battle of Thermopylae on his iPhone. The stereotypes that ancients did embrace rarely line up with contemporary views. Aristotle, for example, did not consider the Greek city-states part of Europe, whose population he dismissed as inferior. People who lived in Europe’s colder regions, he wrote, were “full of spirit but inferior with regard to intelligence and skill,” adding that they lacked “civic organization and the ability to rule their neighbours.” Rome, meanwhile, as the classicist Naoíse Mac Sweeney writes in The West , “ gloried in the idea of itself as a mongrel nation,” tracing its mythical origin, in Virgil’s epic Aeneid , not to Northern Europe, but to Troy, in Asia. As Quinn writes, “As late as the first century BCE some Roman geographers were still unsure whether Europe and Africa were separate continents.” That’s understandable, considering that North African grain kept the empire fed, and “by the 180s CE nearly a third of Roman senators were of African origin.” Basically everyone in the Roman empire was a “polyglot,” Palmer writes. “One heard all sorts of languages in the streets of Rome: Aramaic, Hebrew, etc., with Greek serving as a lingua Franca.” Many of the texts that tell us about these worlds, the supposed blueprints of Western civilization, might have been lost during the Middle Ages, Mac Sweeney points out, if they had not been preserved in places such as the House of Wisdom, the great library in Baghdad that drew scholars from all over the world. C laiming descent from the Roman empire is an ancient, and global, pastime. The citizens of the Eastern Roman empire called themselves Romans, never Byzantines. Once they were defeated by the Ottomans, the sultan took the title kayser-i-rum , or “Caesar of Rome.” The czar of Russia is similarly derived from caesar . Ivan III went so far as to marry the Byzantine princess Sophia Palaiologina to bolster Moscow’s claim to being the “Third Rome.” The Holy Roman Empire put it right there in the name. So many of Trump’s political strategies are intended to make the same case: the “Western civilization” speeches; the landmarks he names after himself; the proposals to colonize Greenland and Canada; the calls for public executions of enemies; the grand ballroom and arch in Washington, D.C. It is a regime legitimization tactic dreamed up by a 10-year-old who wants to grow up to be Roman emperor. [ Listen: Why America isn’t Rome (and why that matters) ] MAGA’s nostalgia for this outdated historiography has been used to back up arguments that demographic change, expansions of civic equality, and political transition threaten the advance of civilization, instead of being the prerequisites for it. Better to throw up walls, tariff your allies and enemies alike, pursue mass deportation, defund and censor scholarship, and wage wars to demonstrate your superior might. In a speech to the Federalist Society this month dismissing the legitimacy of the International Criminal Court, Rubio quoted the Roman general Pompey: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” John Adams was fond of quoting a different Roman, Cicero: “ cedant arma togae ,” or “let arms give way to togas.” The Founders idealized the Roman republic —not the Roman empire, which they saw as a cautionary tale about the death of free societies. Pompey’s quote foreshadows that death—and his own beheading. Rubio’s praise for the rule of arms over the rule of law identifies him as the kind of man the Founders thought had destroyed the republic, instead of defending it. Thomas Jefferson called appeals to force like Rubio’s “the vital principle and immediate parent of despotism.” Judging by the results of the midterms, voters don’t see the Trump era as a new golden age. This administration does share some qualities with ancient Rome—a predilection for oligarchy , public executions , and losing wars to Persia , to name just a few. But the idea of America as the apex of civilization will persist long after MAGA is gone, because people’s identities and the status they derive from those identities are important to them. Stories like these stick because they convey a simple message: We are better . Maybe the we is “Americans.” Maybe it’s Europeans. Maybe it’s men, heterosexuals, Christians, or conservatives. As Rubio put it: “I never said our history is perfect. I have only said our history is better than anybody else’s.” But as Quinn writes, civilizations do not advance through isolation; they advance through exchange. There is no ancient Greece without Phoenicia and Mesopotamia, no ancient Rome without Egypt and Anatolia, and, I would add, no America without African gold and labor . Clearly, these exchanges are not always pleasant or mutually beneficial. War, genocide, slavery, and exploitation are cornerstones of the human experience. Antiquity was not a tolerant, multiracial paradise, but neither is the story of humanity a hero’s journey with the Great White Man as protagonist. Given how human civilization actually advances, the fixation on purity and uniformity is self-destructive. Without change, without dynamism, societies are doomed to decay. Rather than preserving “civilization,” you suffocate your own society like a candle flame in a bell jar.

items.title: Security Council LIVE: Can conflict resolution keep pace as AI and drones reshape war?
items.description: When the UN was founded in 1945, computers, the internet and satellites were the stuff of science fiction. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) is already assisting in targeting, drones are reshaping warfare and disinformation is spreading in unprecedented ways, fuelling record levels of conflict. The Security Council on Tuesday is weighing these changes, with UN chief António Guterres telling ambassadors, “killer robots must have no place in our future.”

items.title: Bafoulabé : une pétition lancée pour la réhabilitation de la route Manantali-Kobri
items.description: Un collectif denomme « Collectif Axe Manantali-Tambaga » a lance, le lundi 23 novembre 2026, une petition en ligne pour reclamer la rehabilitation de la route Manantali-Kobri-Tambaga. Durant tout l'hivernage, la degradation de cet axe a fortement perturbe la circulation et isole plusieurs localites riveraines. Selon les initiateurs, cette mobilisation vise a attirer l'attention sur l'importance de cette route, consideree comme un axe vital pour les populations et le trafic de la premiere region. Elle dessert notamment les cercles de Kita, Sagabari, Bafoulabe et Oussoubidiagna. L’article Bafoulabé : une pétition lancée pour la réhabilitation de la route Manantali-Kobri est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .
